items.title: [Draft] EXL3 Flash Next on CUDA: TP=2, BF16 paging, cache reuse, graphs
items.body:
**Draft for upstream review; not merge-ready.** This ex3-on-upstream-wip/branch/exl3-on-upstream-wip integrates the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next EXL3 path with upstream `main` (base `d1018b318`). It is a broad working draft intended to be split into focused PRs before merge. The implementation has working paths, but required correctness, capacity, and performance gates remain open; in particular, CUDA graphs have not demonstrated a repeatable speedup. ## What it adds - EXL3 weight loading and CUDA execution in TensorFold's Flash Next path. - Routed-expert offload with per-layer GPU pools, pinned host banks, and asynchronous H2D staging. - Opt-in persistent decoder/MTP expert-frequency priors, with private per-model/rank storage, checked reload, adaptive startup decay, pool warming and atomic graceful-stop saves. - Expert-parallel TP=2 with split routed experts, shared-expert execution, vocabulary-sharded `lm_head`, and NCCL collectives. - BF16 KV paging to host RAM, snapshots/restores, and prefix/cache reuse, with an opt-in per-rank shared block arena. Ordinary-context private/shared snapshot and served reuse gates pass; the 200k × 2 target remains unqualified. - MTP drafting and CUDA graph capture/replay. Decode graphs cover eligible rounds/windows; prefill graphs capture dense sub-blocks, while expert scheduling/copies remain eager. These are implemented paths in the branch, not claims that every supported shape or failure mode is validated. The evidence and remaining gates below define what has actually been checked. ## Memory and execution split Configuration shown: **TP=2 with BF16 KV paging enabled** (`TF_FLASHNEXT_KVPAGE=1`). Each request uses both GPUs. The boxes show placement, not allocation sizes. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph HOST["CPU scheduling and host RAM"] direction TB RAM0["Rank 0 RAM

MoE all-reduce
Logit all-gather"] GPU1 <--> NCCL classDef gpu fill:#e8f2ff,stroke:#3765a3,color:#152b46 class GPU0,GPU1 gpu ``` - **Replication and sharding:** paging currently disables attention-head sharding, so each rank has the full attention/KV layout and its own host backing allocation. Decoder routed experts and `lm_head` vocabulary columns remain split. With paging disabled, a separate attention-head split is available; it is not the configuration drawn here. - **Expert movement:** host-planned paths use asynchronous H2D copies. The deep-prefill ring reuses decoder pool storage across layers. In device-planned decode, GPU kernels read mapped host banks to fill cache lines; overflow experts can be read in place. Routed caches retain experts for reuse, while the shared expert has a separate resident allocation on rank 1. CPU scheduling does not mean CPU expert execution. - **KV and snapshots:** selected older KV blocks are fetched into the device block cache; recent window rows are written back to RAM during window rebasing or snapshot flushing. Snapshots preserve host KV history, device windows/cache contents, pager tables, and recurrent/PLE/MTP state where present. The PLE table itself is file-backed; gathered embeddings are uploaded. - **Shared block option:** `TF_FLASHNEXT_KVPAGE_SHARED=1` uses one block pool per rank with fixed per-lane windows and generation-tagged ownership. Private per-sequence paging remains the default. Shared version-2 snapshots retain only owned blocks and remap them into destination slots; they do not overwrite the whole arena or deduplicate identical-prefix payloads. Capacity pooling can trade cache hits for VRAM, so it is not a throughput claim. - **Scope:** the NCCL box denotes logical communication, not a direct GPU peer link. Memory budgets depend on configuration. Ordinary-context TP=2 paging/cache behavior has been exercised; 200k × 2 with paged KV remains unproven. Prefill expert scheduling/copies remain eager when dense prefill graphs are enabled. ## Proposed PR segmentation This is a proposed split plan, not a claim that the listed PRs already exist. Each future PR should own one coherent layer, add focused tests, and record its correctness and performance evidence. Until then, this mega PR remains a tracking draft and should not be merged as one piece. The current branch already contains prototype implementations for these areas; the listed gates are remaining review/acceptance criteria. 1. **EXL3 foundation and resident forward:** isolate format/config parsing, weight loading, and the upstream CUDA adapter. Acceptance: layer/model oracle gates for the resident path. 2. **Expert pool and offload:** isolate host-bank layout, device line pools, replacement policy, async copies, and pool lifecycle. Acceptance: pooled output matches resident execution; measure copy/compute overlap rather than assuming it. 3. **TP=2 execution and serving:** isolate expert partitioning, shared-expert placement, vocabulary-head split, collectives, and rank lifecycle. Acceptance: TP=2 logits/outputs meet a defined numerical tolerance and the server works on both GPUs. 4. **BF16 KV paging and state reuse:** isolate device/host page tables, paging/eviction, paged snapshots/restores, and prefix branching. Acceptance: paged/resident equivalence where comparable; exact state/logit parity for snapshot/restore and cache reuse, plus long-context tests. 5. **MTP drafting:** isolate draft-head input, TP=2 draft/verify, and prompt-cache interaction. Acceptance: committed drafted tokens equal serial decoding with drafting disabled. 6. **CUDA graph decode:** isolate stable graph inputs/outputs, TP=2 collectives, offload boundaries, and capture/replay lifecycle. Acceptance: graph/eager output equality over repeated replay and snapshot restore. 7. **CUDA graph prefill and scheduling:** isolate chunked capture, expert-major scheduling, staging overlap, and profiling-driven tuning. Acceptance: repeatable graph-on improvement in controlled prefill/decode measurements without correctness or memory regressions. 8. **Final capacity and product integration:** run repeated 200k-context × 2-concurrency TP=2 tests with BF16 paging/cache reuse, resource margin, and failure cleanup; then consider family/recipe registration. Do not register until preceding gates pass. Proposed dependencies: the foundation precedes the other slices; expert offload and TP=2 build on it; paging needs stable TP=2 allocation/lifecycle; MTP needs TP=2 and cache semantics; graph work depends on stable paging/offload and eager behavior. Decode and prefill graph slices can be developed in parallel once interfaces are fixed, but should be integrated and reviewed in dependency order. Avoid duplicate implementations: use stacked branches or clean cherry-picks, and keep this umbrella draft as an index until the sequence is complete. ## Benchmark report The detailed tables, exact tested commit, model/checkpoint identity, runtime configuration and methodology are in the [21 October benchmark comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6315696853). These historical results apply to source `ca2b13c88315c9c1c7a9ce17c002226f3585f73a`, not subsequent candidate changes. The single matched graph/eager run did not establish a speedup. ## Evidence and remaining gates - **Prior replay/cache correctness checkpoint:** runtime `4afc6169` passes 192 EXL3 host tests, real native/GPU-runner builds, private/shared buffer-reuse/snapshot checks on both cards, and exact TP2 prefill origin/grid rebinding through dense/sparse and paging-split transitions. The native MTP/graph/shared-BF16 cold/warm/branch/rewind gate retains all eight reference hashes. [Exact sources, binaries, model, methodology and scope](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792). Correctness-run timings overlapping compilation are excluded; isolated graph speedup remains unproven. Retaining buffers does not retain old-owner graphs. - **Prior replay/cache telemetry checkpoint:** runtime `975c1df9` passes 177 EXL3 host tests, the native CUDA build, diagnostics-enabled TP2 shared-BF16 cache reuse with separate valid expert/KV counters, and diagnostics-disabled c8 hash/replay qualification. Source `b3a7b565` also passes the focused real TP2 width-3/4/16 rebind fixture. [Full source, model, methodology and bounded measurements](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6327563987). Those receipts do not qualify subsequent runtime changes. No repeatable speedup, independent golden fidelity or 200k capacity is inferred. - **New shared BF16 checkpoint:** historical runtime [`ccb32fc3`](https://github.com/BlivionIaG/TensorFold/commit/ccb32fc3ba313bbde74401e305f572234c9bbe81); these direct fixture results are not relabeled as current-head tests. 153 EXL3 host tests and real native/GPU-test CUDA builds pass. Matched TP=2 private/shared sparse-paging fixtures pass exact restored-state checks, owned-entry remapping, recycled/asymmetric generations, foreign-request isolation and actual prefill/decode graph replay. Two 16,424-token HTTP histories with MTP and graphs pass cold/warm/branch/rewind reuse against the private reference. The [full qualification comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6325790752) separates these tests from the earlier same-binary `0de41d37` allocation measurement (920 MiB lower sampled peaks per GPU). Shared mode stays opt-in; none of these results establishes independent model fidelity, repeatable graph speedup or 200k × 2 capacity. - **Served BF16 paging/cache gate on `ca2b13c8`:** two concurrent HTTP histories, each with 16,424 prompt tokens and 32 generated tokens, passed cold, warm, branch and rewind phases with graphs and MTP enabled. Full response hashes matched a separately started cache-disabled reference for every phase. Cache-enabled requests reused 16,407–16,417 tokens on warm/branch/rewind phases; warm native prefill times were 0.944 / 0.974 seconds. This proves ordinary-length prefix reuse and continuation parity, not long-context capacity, independent model fidelity, or exact internal-state parity at this new head. - **Completed matched graph/eager gate on `ca2b13c8`:** all four exact 1024/512 and 16384/1024 cases at c1/c8 passed in each mode (36 valid responses, 18/18 matching full token/text hashes). Binary and per-rank expert geometry were identical. Both ranks replayed decoder graphs while all eight requests decoded in each c8 cell, and replayed prefill graphs in the long-input cells. Graph-run physical GPU peaks were 14,958 / 14,996 MiB; automatic expert pools were 10 / 23 lines per layer. This is an ordinary-context functional/capacity pass, not a 200k claim. - **21 October checkpoint:** source `ca2b13c8` is integrated without rewriting the draft history. The parent EXL3 host gate passes 90/90 tests, scoped formatting/diff checks pass, all tracked source hashes match the Linux build tree, and the native CUDA sm_120 build succeeds. This adds workload-scaled graph budgets, class-aware local graph charges, selective coordinated TP LRU retirement, and a tested local-reclamation fallback. Graph memory charges remain heuristic, not measured exec sizes. - **New snapshot hardware receipt:** on the preceding `d3662d1b` runtime with test-only upstream loader compatibility fixes, both RTX 5060 Ti ranks passed the compiled two-lane BF16-paged snapshot fixture. Restored canonical KV history, recurrent/index/PLE state and continuation logits matched exactly. Each graph iteration recorded 27 prefill and 5 decode replays per rank. This uses 24 expert lines per layer and no MTP head; it is not an eight-lane capacity, served prefix-cache, or 200k test. The new checkpoint separately passes the served cache-reuse gate below; this older direct state/logit fixture is not relabeled as a current-tree run. - **Performance remains an acceptance blocker:** graph decode was 3.4–5.4% slower across the four cells in this single matched pair. No repeatable speedup is established. Cache-key churn and the graph/expert/KV memory partition remain optimization work; increasing reserved memory is not itself a performance fix. The earlier interrupted diagnostic overlapped compilation and is not a controlled performance receipt. - On earlier source-tree revisions, TP=2 serving, draft-on/off output parity, BF16 paging, snapshot/cache reuse, and graph/eager correctness were exercised on development hardware. These results are not a full validation of the exact current PR head. - CUDA graphs currently match eager in tested paths, but controlled profiling has not established a graph-on speedup. That is a hard performance gate, not a claimed win. - The strict golden-prompt near-tie and remaining TP numerical-parity questions still require closure. - Ordinary-context TP=2 private/shared paging, scoped state/logit restoration, graph replay and served cache reuse now pass on runtime `ccb32fc3` as described in the qualification comment. Cancellation/overflow/live-rank failure injection, repeated performance qualification and the 200k × 2 BF16 paging target remain required before merge/registration. The earlier near-200k × 2 retrieval test used resident BF16 KV and is not evidence for paged-KV capacity. - Fresh `tools/zig/lean_check.py` run: 1,762 findings on the current source versus 444 on pinned upstream `d1018b318` (1,318 more). This remains a CONTRIBUTING blocker, not a clean result. - CPU expert execution is out of scope. BF16 remains the required KV-cache format; int8 KV is not part of the serving path. Branch: `exl3-on-upstream-wip` Current fork head: `0272aafe266299c078976c74fbe5347bdf484f7c` (qualified target-layer history, DMA coalescing, opt-in transfer provenance and actual-layer GDN graph keys; bounded TP2 BF16 cache/parity and screening measurements pass) Upstream base: `d1018b318fb51981c4a18f12e40269a4d3ee9713` ### Persistent expert-profile checkpoint (22 October) Native source `babc9762e2dbc999c9b68df252d619830203d693`, binary SHA-256 `86a7b20b6bac2bc5b2b78f9c89654a21cd1c0bd2ad9e6806ee1dc70abe110907`, passes a real TP2 graceful stop/start gate with graphs, MTP and shared BF16 paging: two waves of two concurrent 1,024-input/64-output requests in each fresh process pair, prefix cache off, fixed pools 32/48. Both ranks save, reload, warm and update their profiles; response hashes match across restart. The leader is signalled and the existing TP stop protocol releases the follower. Startup warms 1,568 / 2,304 existing lines, with no pool enlargement. The profile checkpoint also passes 211 host tests and 15 focused Linux Debug/ReleaseSafe persistence tests; a separate source-53ef CUDA fixture verifies actual bytes/tables and resized pool restart on both GPUs. Enable with `TF_FLASHNEXT_EXL3_PROFILE_DIR`. The advisory fingerprint covers routed trellis plus config/index bytes, not every checkpoint tensor; hashing costs about 16.6 seconds per rank at startup in this gate. Counts are decayed once and saved by replacement, not added twice. The separate deep-prefill ring histogram is not persisted; prefill may discard startup residency. Abrupt follower/process kills can lose unsaved updates. These are placement priors, not KV snapshots or elastic budgeting. A separate short-prompt ABBA with drafts off measured 9.0% lower TTFT and 6.5% lower decode latency for warm versus cold persisted profiles (TP=2, graphs and BF16 paging on; 128-token input / 64-token greedy output; identical full output hashes). This narrow result is not evidence for long-context or drafted-serving gains, nor a graph speedup; profile fingerprinting adds about 16.6 seconds of startup per rank. Full methodology and values are in the [final report](https://github.com/BlivionIaG/TensorFold/blob/exl3-on-upstream-wip/docs/plans/exl3-on-upstream-final-report.md). No independent golden-fidelity, long-prefill-speed or 200k×2 gate is closed by this test. ### Latest prefill efficiency candidate `ce10271d` starts initial expert copies before CPU member-list construction and coalesces copy-stream dependencies for equal/older release epochs, preserving newer-reader and event-wrap guards. It passes 215 EXL3 host tests, native CUDA host/forward-body compilation, formatting/diff checks and zero new lean findings. **Native TP2 BF16 cold/warm/branch/rewind parity now passes for the specified ce10271d workload; the matched ce/babc revision comparison is effectively flat. Independent model fidelity and 200k capacity are not inferred.** Previous hardware receipts apply only to their named sources. Copy-grid-only tuning (144/36/36/144, frozen native `babc9762`, TP2 c2, 1k/256, two waves/server) was 0.3–0.5% slower in both ordered pairs with exact response parity; the default stays unchanged. ### Latest measured follow-up `a25fa226` passes a real native TP2 gate with two concurrent 16,424-token histories, MTP, prefill/decode graph replay, BF16 RAM paging and prefix reuse at 4096-row prefill. All eight cold/warm/branch/rewind outputs match the separate cold reference. Demand/initial-prefetch/cross-layer-prefetch copy and requested-byte categories reconcile on both ranks. Native SHA256: `939f5ef182c9bfefb1efe2a3847715c32011b734f703427a52a311ada61df5bf`; 222 EXL3 +218 runtime host tests pass, zero new lean findings. The previous `ce10271d` revision showed no meaningful speedup against its baseline. Profiling identified expert-transfer volume and many separate projection DMA submissions. The new direct-copy helper combines projections only with proven common pinned-bank provenance and exact adjacency, with guarded fallback; no CUDA arithmetic or graph ownership checks were weakened. The matched ce/a25 code comparison at identical4096-row settings is complete and shows no repeatable gain; one pair has worse decode/ITL. A subsequent matching-target-layer-history candidate passes native cache parity and all16 benchmark hashes/replay checks in four fresh A/B/B/A servers, with about2.1% aggregate decode-service improvement in both screening pairs and only0.2–0.3% effective-prefill improvement. It is integrated with unchanged mandatory loading and graph/BF16-paging guards;227 host tests and native compilation pass. Two pairs do not establish statistical significance or causal graph/eager speedup; diagnostic total transfer volume is effectively unchanged. Tested source and binary, exact ratios and the separate current-default CUDA profile are recorded in the linked measurement comment. A separate four-fresh-server setting comparison shows 4096 versus forced2048 rows improves TTFT about39% and effective aggregate-prefill about64% on the stated TP2/c2 workload, with exact hashes and actual graph reuse. **4096 is already the engine default; the inherited benchmark harness forced2048. This is a setting comparison, not a new-code gain.** The8192 pilot is not accepted because cached-prefill replay failed its unchanged gate. Cross-request graph retention remains disabled pending complete captured-allocation lifetime proof. Full methodology, exact tested commits, units and limits are in the [existing measurement comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792). ### Dense EXL3 prompt-kernel update (22 October; pushed head `5a94359c07c8f716255ff9b0de7a7257dec1432f`) A Blackwell sm120+ mul1/C2 `ldmatrix.x4` input-fragment path is now included. The four fresh-server A/B/B/A TP2 screening pairs with 16,384 input / 256 output, c2, graphs/MTP, BF16 RAM paging, 4096-row prefill and pools 32/48 show effective aggregate-prefill +2.27%/+2.23% and TTFT −2.28%/−2.24%; aggregate decode-service +0.77%/+1.23%. All response hashes match. This is a small two-pair screening result, not statistical significance or graph/eager causality. The canonical candidate passes the BF16 paging/cache cold/warm/branch/rewind gate (8/8 responses) and changed-kernel CUDA/resource checks. Full kernel-contract timed out at 300 seconds on both GPUs; broad contract pass is not claimed. Exact methods, hashes, limits and assessment of the reviewer’s cache/page-table pointers are in the latest [measurement comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/1113#issuecomment-6328093792).

items.body:
**Draft for upstream review; not merge-ready.** This is the working line for serving the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next EXL3 pack on two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GiB cards, based on current upstream `main`. The immediate goal is a working, optimized implementation; this deliberately broad draft will be split into focused PRs before merge.

## What it adds

- EXL3 loading and CUDA execution in TensorFold's Flash Next path.
- Routed-expert offload with per-layer GPU pools, pinned host banks, and asynchronous H2D staging.
- Expert-parallel TP=2 with split routed experts, shared-expert execution, vocabulary-sharded `lm_head`, and NCCL collectives.
- BF16 KV paging to host RAM, snapshot/restore, and prefix/cache reuse.
- MTP drafting, plus CUDA graph capture/replay for decode and prefill paths.

## Proposed PR segmentation

The PRs should be split and reviewed in dependency order; each PR owns one coherent layer, includes focused tests, and records correctness and performance evidence. Until then, this mega PR remains a tracking draft and should not be merged as one piece.

1. **EXL3 foundation and resident forward:** format/config parsing, real weight loading, upstream CUDA adapter, and layer/model oracle gates. This establishes a correct non-offloaded path.
2. **Expert pool and offload:** host-bank layout, device line pools, replacement policy, asynchronous copies, and pool lifecycle tests. Gate: pooled output matches resident execution; document copy/compute overlap.
3. **TP=2 execution and serving:** expert partitioning, shared-expert placement, vocabulary head split, collectives, and rank lifecycle. Gate: TP=2 logits/outputs match the defined numerical tolerance and server works on both GPUs.
4. **BF16 KV paging and state reuse:** device/host page tables, paging/eviction, snapshots that preserve paged state, restore, and prefix branching. Gate: paged equals resident; snapshot/restore and cache reuse preserve exact state/logits, including long-context tests.
5. **MTP drafting:** draft head fed from real logits, TP=2 draft/verify path, and prompt-cache interaction. Gate: drafted committed tokens equal serial decoding with drafting disabled.
6. **CUDA graph decode:** stable graph inputs/outputs, TP=2 collectives, expert-offload boundaries, capture/replay lifecycle, and snapshot restore. Gate: graph and eager outputs match across replay and recovery.
7. **CUDA graph prefill and scheduling:** chunked prefill capture, expert-major scheduling, staging overlap, and profiling-driven tuning. Gate: graph-on improves controlled prefill/decode measurements without correctness or memory regressions.
8. **Final capacity and product integration:** repeated 200k-context × 2-concurrency TP=2 runs with BF16 paging/cache reuse, resource margin, failure cleanup, then family/recipe registration. Registration stays out until all preceding gates pass.

Dependencies: PR 1 precedes the rest; PRs 2 and 3 build on it; PR 4 needs stable TP=2 allocation/lifecycle; PR 5 needs TP=2 and cache semantics; graph PRs depend on stable paging/offload and eager behavior. The graph decode and prefill PRs may be developed in parallel after those interfaces are fixed, then merged in that order. Do not create eight duplicate implementations: use stacked branches or cherry-pick cleanly after each preceding PR lands, and keep the umbrella draft as an index until the sequence is complete.

## Evidence and remaining gates

- TP=2 serving, draft-on/off parity, BF16 paging, snapshots/cache reuse, and graph/eager correctness have been exercised on development hardware on earlier source-tree revisions.
- CUDA graphs currently match eager in tested paths, but controlled profiling has not established a graph-on speedup. That is a hard performance gate, not a claimed win.
- The strict golden-prompt near-tie and remaining TP numerical-parity questions still require closure.
- Re-run the full TP=2, snapshot/restore, cache-reuse, graph-prefill/decode, and 200k × 2 gates on the current branch before merge or model registration.
- `tools/zig/lean_check.py` reports 1,317 findings beyond upstream `main`; this remains a CONTRIBUTING blocker.
- CPU expert execution is out of scope. BF16 remains the required KV-cache format; int8 KV is not part of the serving path.

items.title: Flash Next on CUDA: the qwen4_exp family on the native CUDA host, every stream through the lane rounds
items.body:
## What this changes

Adds a CUDA engine for Qwen3.8 Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) to `tensorfold-native`: an MLX affine 4-bit, group-32
checkpoint with its MTP head, served through the core's lane rounds, lane host and prompt cache, with drafted windows,
shared rounds, kept prompt states and prompt chunks between other streams' rounds. Every kernel it launches is built
from this repository, so it boots with no capture. `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS` can name a captured set of the Python
0.6.1 engine's Triton kernels, which then stands in for our glue so its tokens can be compared with that engine's
teacher path; `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED` swaps single entry points back to ours beside a set. It builds on @AdrianBinDC's
#476 and answers #472. His commits are here with his authorship and messages, rebased onto `main` with #835's cache
guard (027ddea9): five needed their `zig/build/cuda.zig` or `zig/tests/cuda/copies.py` hunks fitted to what `main` has
now, and his formatting commit is left out, since `main` has the same line from his 7bbe2208.

Following `docs/recipes/adding-a-zig-family.md` and CONTRIBUTING.md:30-31, the family supplies its config check, weight
map, layer graph and kernels for what is its own; shared pieces are the core's:

- the round loop, verify/accept and the lane host schedule every token; the family adds no scheduler;
- the prompt cache's store and rules keep and resume states; the family copies a stream's state (with the MTP head's
  rows for a drafting stream, lookahead 1 as Nemotron);
- prompts run a chunk a call through the core's `prefill_step`;
- shared row kernels: token rows (`embed_rows.cu`, now in groups of 32 with a copy a stream), RMS rows with their group
  sums (`norms.cu`, the MTP head's norms), a new `route_rows.cu` for router logits and softmax top-k with a shared
  gate, and the routed experts over a window's rows on the core's plan (`cuda/grouped.zig`) and a new core lane kernel,
  `experts_rows.cu` (`cuda.experts.RowsExperts`), which gives every row the decode kernel's sums;
- the family's own kernels: the hyper-connections and the n-gram gate and conv (`flashnext_hc.cu`), attention with its
  output gate and the sparse indexer's pooling and scores (`flashnext_attn.cu`), the indexer's block selection and the
  Gated DeltaNet chain (`flashnext_batch.cu`), and the MTP head;
- shards are read with `core.safetensors.File`; a captured set is packed with `tools/zig/triton_aot_pack.py` and
  launched through `cuda.aot.Set`.

Every kernel keeps a row's own sums in a fixed order, so a row's bits are the same at any row count: drafted windows
equal serial decoding, rounds equal lone streams, resumed prompts equal fresh ones. Our glue rounds to bf16 where the
Python engine's kernels do, with IEEE division and square root and the core's within-one-ulp exp (`glue_math.cuh`);
the router and the hyper-connections' 4-bit dots run on mma tiles with K in ascending order.

Commits:
- @AdrianBinDC's 22 commits from #476: the embedding, every layer type and the final mix matched to the Python engine's
  host checks one by one, then a drafts-off prompt token for token.
- The token-id and position uploads go on the compute stream, and attention runs over every 512-key chunk a prompt has.
- `native/cuda.zig` reads a family's prompt-cache copies, cache rules and device weight bytes from what it declares
  (Nemotron's paths unchanged); Flash Next registers.
- Core: `experts_rows.cu` and `tf-cuda-test experts-rows`.
- Core: `triton_aot_pack.py` leaves out constexprs Triton folded from `None` and takes a `--jit` per capture.
- The engine on one batched pass (prompts and decode rounds), the sparse indexer and the 262,144-token window.
- The MTP head, its chains, verify windows and the DeltaNet rollback.
- The lane backend: drafted windows, shared rounds, kept prompt states (drafting streams too), prompt steps.
- A sequence's buffers are zeroed on the compute stream (a fill with no stream raced the first pass).
- The config check refuses semantic settings the kernels fix (RMS epsilon, RoPE, gate and activation types, layer
  roles, the n-gram layer), by field name.
- A failed zero fill frees the buffer it was filling.
- A pass's uploads read pinned staging the scratch owns until the copies land.
- Core: `route_rows.cu` (router logits on mma tiles, softmax top-k with a shared gate) with `core/route_ref.zig` and
  `tf-cuda-test route-rows`.
- Core: token rows in groups of 32 with copies, and RMS rows with their group sums; `norm-rows` covers both.
- Our glue, `flashnext_hc.cu` and `flashnext_attn.cu`, with `tf-cuda-test flashnext-hc` and `flashnext-attn`.
- The engine boots on our glue; a captured set that holds every entry point is used for comparison; `flashnext-compare`.
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED`, our glue for the named entry points beside a captured set.
- Docs: `docs/recipes/flash-next-cuda.md`, the Flash Next, CUDA and recipe-index pages, RUNBOOK, CHANGELOG.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `flashnext-cuda` 7746bb9d on 027ddea9 (`main` c7137bb3, v1.0.11 + 19, with #835's cache guard),
  Zig 0.17.0; NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121), driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0.88, Ubuntu 24.04.5; checkpoint

- Not run: Metal (no change there; the Mac Flash Next host is untouched), sm_86 and sm_120 cards (none here), CUDA

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo.
- [x] No precision traded for speed. If the bits change, the description says which sums change and why. Ours against
  the captured kernels: `_embed`, `_router`, `_pool` and `_scores` give the same bits; the others change at the ulp
  level, from IEEE division and square root and a within-one-ulp exp where Triton uses its approximate forms (the
  norms' 1/sqrt, sigmoid, SiLU and softmax exps, the output gate), from fixed-order block and warp sums where Triton
  reduces in its own tree (the write-back's and n-gram gate's squared sums, the group sums the 4-bit dots take, the
  attention rows' p sums), from attention tiles of 32 keys where Triton's are 64 (the online softmax rescales at other
  points), from explicit fused multiply-adds in the dots' epilogues and the merge, and from sincosf with full range
  reduction for RoPE. Which tokens that moves is in the receipt.
- [ ] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release. (No release has this engine; against the captured set a
  cold 12,001-token prompt is 1% slower, 10.40 s against 10.30 s.)
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran, Metal M1 to M5 and CUDA, and which I could not. (GB10 only.)
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency.
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

## Not in this PR, said plainly

- Our glue's tokens are not the Python engine's teacher path's on every prompt: on the 3,001-token prompt they part at
  token 15. The captured set, given by `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS`, still gives that path's tokens (32/32 on all five).
- Dense projections run #476's copy of the Python engine's group-32 lane matmul (`qmm.cu`); the core's `qmm_group` and
  `lane_gemv` are built for groups of 64. I have not checked whether a group-32 `qmm_group` instance gives the same bits.
- No CUDA graphs and no GPU-side rounds. Drafted streams verify their windows one batched pass each, so drafted
  throughput does not grow with streams, and the MTP head drafts one stream at a time (Nemotron batches them, #768).
- Prompts are slower than the Python engine's: a cold 12,001-token prompt takes 10.4 s here against 6.7 s there.
- Draws are made on the host from each row's scores (a 248,320-wide bf16 row a token).
- int8 KV is not in this PR; bf16 only.
- Checked on a GB10 only; the kernels build for the release SMs but have not run on sm_86 or sm_120.
- The core's `DeviceBuffer.fill8(..., null)` returns before the memset lands on device memory and is not ordered with a
  non-blocking stream. This PR stops Flash Next using it; a doc line on `fill8` may save the next family the same hunt.

items.title: MiniMax H3 / FastH3 on CUDA in the checkpoint's bf16, one GPU or several Sparks over RoCE
items.body:
**Thank you, Ash, for the review of #585 and #947, and for the runtime this builds on.**

**H3's 50 blocks now run on TensorFold's CUDA runtime at the checkpoint's own precision, and the same pass splits across DGX Sparks with the bits of one GPU.**
- bf16 weights as shipped, bf16 activations, fp32 sums, fp32 softmax and fp32 routing.
- The products are the runtime's own cuBLASLt `Linear` (`zig/src/cuda/cublaslt.zig`: fp32 compute, no TF32).
- Ranks trade bf16 keys and values.
- Nothing is quantized, and int8 is gone from the family.

This answers #585's objection ("the int8 projections and attention are also a precision trade we don't make anywhere in the engine"). It is the CUDA half of #949, the Metal bf16 version: the same routing in fp32, the same kernel set, and its float64 references ported. The two read as one family on both backends.

The receipts are for the same machines and clip as #947: a 5 s clip at 864x480, 124 frames, 15,433 rows and 8 passes, on DGX Spark (GB10). The reference is ComfyUI's own bf16 blocks.
- **Parity, far tighter than int8.** All 50 blocks, dense, first pass, against ComfyUI's bf16 blocks on the same rows: cosine **0.99910**, relative error **0.042**. int8 (#947) was 0.99669 and 0.081. One block: cosine 0.99999, relative error 0.0032 (int8 0.0150).
- **Closer to an fp32 forward than the reference itself.** An independent fp32 implementation of the blocks, on the same rows, puts this library at relative error **0.0354** after 50 blocks and ComfyUI's bf16 blocks at **0.0445**.
- **Bit-identical across ranks.** 8 of 8 pass streams match by sha256 at 1, 2 and 3 Sparks, and again after a restart.
- **Speed, per pass:**
  - one GB10: **10.3 s**, against 10.6 s (dense) and 11.1 s (sparse) for the reference;
  - two Sparks: **6.3 s**, 1.7x the reference;
  - three Sparks: **4.9–5.1 s**, 2.1x the reference.
  - The clip takes 101 s, 69 s and 58.5 s.
  - bf16 is slower than int8 (#947: 6.7, 4.1 and 3.0 s). One GPU is bound by its bf16 tensor-core rate: the products run at 85–94 TFLOPS and take 7.5 of the 10.3 s.
- **Kernel contract: every H3 kernel registered.** 11 of 11 H3 kernels pass gates 1–4, including the routing, norm, head, pool, top-k and mix kernels that #947 left out. 0 limit problems on sm_80, 86, 89, 120 and 121.
- **Lean check:** 517 on `main`, 517 here. `zig build test` passes.
- **A rendered clip** matches the int8 and reference clips by eye. Whisper hears the spoken line in all three.

Stacked on #947; the commits of this change alone are https://github.com/drowzeys/TensorFold/compare/upstream/h3-cuda-parallel...upstream/h3-cuda-bf16. If you would rather take one change, the two squash cleanly into a bf16-only family. The int8 variant stays on the fork.

## Why bf16 only, and not bf16 beside int8

- It is the precision the engine keeps everywhere, and what CONTRIBUTING asks for: the checkpoint's activation precision and fp32 accumulation.
- One path means one set of kernels to review and keep under the contract. The int8 products, the quantizer and the saved `.tf-int8` copy are gone: 987 lines out, 497 in, in the family and its kernels.
- #949 makes the same choice on Metal.
- int8's only advantage is speed. The multi-Spark split recovers that without a precision trade.

## What changed

- **`zig/src/families/h3/`:**
  - `cuda_weights.zig` copies the checkpoint's bf16 block tensors to the device as stored (42 GB). `tf_h3_set_weight` copies a host-merged bf16 projection in.
  - `cuda_gemm.zig` (new) holds the products on the runtime's `Linear`. Each (outputs, inputs) shape keeps the algorithm cuBLASLt picks at 16,384 rows, so a rank's rows sum in the same order as on one GPU. That is what keeps ranks bit-identical.
  - `cuda.zig` holds the forward. The dense pass skips the routing gate's product.
  - `cuda_tp.zig` handles the exchange: bf16 keys and values, plus fp32 key and value means when routing.
- **`zig/kernels/cuda/h3.cu`, `h3_attention.cuh`:**
  - The rows: modulated norm, gated adds, SwiGLU and head layout. They round to bf16 where torch's bf16 ops round in the reference.
  - Routing in fp32: tile means, tile scores, top-k and the pooled branch.
  - The tile-routed attention on `mma.sync m16n8k16`: bf16 q, k and v, fp32 scores and online softmax. The weights are rounded to bf16 for the value product, as flash attention does. Q, K and V take 48 KiB, so two blocks fit on an SM, and V's load overlaps the scores.
- **`zig/tests/cuda/contract_h3*.zig`:** nine kernels against their float64 formulas (the Metal family's references, ported), and the top-k against a CPU oracle under a stated rule: a NaN score ranks as −inf, and ties go to the lower tile. `h3_spans` is as before. `registry.zig` holds 11 records.
- **`docs/recipes/minimax-h3-cuda.md`:** the arithmetic and the receipt.

The library's C API is unchanged except that `tf_h3_open` takes the checkpoint alone; there is no saved copy. The lane core and the server are untouched.

## Receipts

**Environment:**
- DGX Spark: GB10, cc 12.1, driver 580.173.02, CUDA 13.0.88, cuBLASLt 13.1.1.3, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-1029-nvidia.
- This branch at `96f0aa2e`, on #947's `b570b8f0`, on `main` `46a08c18`.
- Host ComfyUI `a4b5a045` (0.39.0).
- Checkpoint `FastVideo/FastVideo-FastH3-Comfy` `fastvideo_fasth3_8step_v2_pruned_bf16.safetensors`.
- 864x480, 124 frames, 8 passes, sparsity 0.8, seeds 7 (gate) and 8 (timed).
- Rank 0 is the same machine for every row; ranks talk over RoCE on two rails.
- One model process per GPU, under a MemAvailable kill guard.

| Blocks | A pass | Sampler, 8 passes | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| ComfyUI's bf16 blocks, dense (reference, from #947) | 10.6 s | 85.1 s | 103.0 s |
| ComfyUI's bf16 blocks, its sparse attention 0.8 | 11.1 s | 92.8 s | 111.4 s |
| #947 int8, 1 GPU (rerun today) | 6.61–6.72 s | 54.0 s | 72.4 s |
| **This library, 1 GPU** | **10.27–10.41 s** | **82.8 s** | **101.1 s** |
| **This library, 2 GB10s** | **6.26–6.42 s** | **51.2 s** | **69.4 s** |
| **This library, 3 GB10s** | **4.92–5.06 s** | **40.3 s** | **58.5 s** |

For comparison, #947's int8 on 2 and 3 GB10s: 4.06–4.14 s and 3.02–3.06 s a pass. bf16 doubles the bytes exchanged, about 1.0 s of a 3-rank pass against int8's 0.6 s.

Where one GPU's pass goes, profiled on the library alone:

| Stage | s | Stage | s |
|---|---|---|---|
| q, k, v and gate product | 2.53 | attention out product | 0.69 |
| head layout | 0.48 | MLP in (product + SwiGLU) | 2.87 |
| routing | 0.31 | MLP out product | 1.42 |
| attention | 1.47 | norms, gate mix | 0.48 |

**Bit-identity:**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 2 ranks against 1, 8 passes, seed 7 | 8 of 8 pass streams sha256-identical |
| 3 ranks against 1 | 8 of 8 identical |
| 1 GPU after a ComfyUI restart | 8 of 8 identical |

**Parity.** All rows are measured on the first pass's rows with dense attention. The case was dumped from ComfyUI and replayed through each library on the same machine. Errors are relative L2. Worst row and worst column are the relative errors of the worst single row and channel.

| Against | Blocks | Cosine | Rel. error | Max abs (of values up to) | Worst row | Worst column |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ComfyUI bf16 | 1, **this** | 0.99999 | **0.0032** | 256 (1.08e5) | 0.020 | 0.015 |
| ComfyUI bf16 | 1, int8 #947 | 0.99989 | 0.0150 | 512 | 0.077 | 0.128 |
| ComfyUI bf16 | 50, **this** | **0.99910** | **0.0424** | 2.3e5 (6.2e6) | 0.547 | 0.220 |
| ComfyUI bf16 | 50, int8 #947 | 0.99669 | 0.0813 | 7.9e5 | 0.561 | 0.897 |
| fp32 forward | 1, ComfyUI bf16 | 0.99999 | 0.0052 | 558 | 0.022 | 0.026 |
| fp32 forward | 1, **this** | 0.99999 | **0.0050** | 558 | 0.016 | 0.025 |
| fp32 forward | 50, ComfyUI bf16 | 0.99901 | 0.0445 | 1.3e5 | 0.328 | 0.228 |
| fp32 forward | 50, **this** | 0.99937 | **0.0354** | 2.9e5 | 0.341 | 0.178 |
| fp32 forward | 50, int8 #947 | 0.99714 | 0.0756 | 7.3e5 | 0.382 | 0.887 |

The fp32 forward is an independent torch implementation of the blocks: fp32 weights and activations, no TF32, SDPA's memory-efficient fp32 kernel. It shares no code with ComfyUI or this library. Against it, this library's aggregate and worst-column errors are below ComfyUI's own. Its worst row is slightly above (0.341 against 0.328).

**Memory**, the library alone: `tf_h3_open` on the checkpoint, then three passes over the 15,433-row geometry, sampled every 0.5 s.

| | Device (nvidia-smi peak) | MemAvailable drop |
|---|---|---|
| 1 GPU, every tile | 44,253 MiB (bf16 block weights 40,426) | 45,746 MiB |
| 1 of 2 ranks, 144 tiles, 3 GiB region | 42,870 MiB | 47,322 MiB |

int8 needed 23,052 MiB. The process maps the checkpoint while it copies the tensors, so its resident pages peak at 36–38 GB during the load. It ran beside ComfyUI with its own checkpoint mapped and its text encoder resident, on a 128 GB Spark.

**Clips** (seed 7 fox, frames at 2.5 s and 4 s; and a spoken line, seed 11). Left to right: this library, #947 int8, ComfyUI's bf16 blocks. All three are clean and coherent, and differ only as sparse routing does. Whisper (small, English) heard "The last train leaves at nine tonight." from all three speech clips.

![Fox, left to right: bf16 here, #947 int8, ComfyUI bf16](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drowzeys/TensorFold/pr-assets/h3-bf16-fox.png)

![Spoken line, same order](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/drowzeys/TensorFold/pr-assets/h3-bf16-speech.png)

Commands:

```sh
zig build tf-h3 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc
zig build kernel-contract -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc
zig build fatbins kernel-contract-fatbins -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc -Dsm=80,86,89,120,121
tf-cuda-test kernel-contract-limits zig-out/fatbin
```

The clip timings came from the Studio's ComfyUI node, as in #947. Parity used a case dump of the first pass, replayed through each library's `tf_h3_forward_host`. The ranks ran the Studio's `rank.py`, and the memory figures came from its `bench.py`. These are app-side harnesses and are not part of this change.

## Kernel contract

```
SUMMARY 23 kernels: 23 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail, 0 known findings; 5 controls: 5 red as planted, 0 missed; 0 limit problems; gates 47300 ms, limits 1 ms
PASS kernel-contract-limits: every registered launch fits sm_80, sm_86, sm_89, sm_120 and sm_121, every control red
```

The H3 kernels are `h3_norm`, `h3_gate_add`, `h3_gate_mix`, `h3_swiglu`, `h3_heads`, `h3_pool`, `h3_tile_scores`, `h3_coarse`, `h3_attention`, `h3_topk` and `h3_spans`.
- Each is checked against its formula in float64.
- Intermediate bf16 roundings are declared as `mids`, and inputs are one-signed where a sum could cancel.
- Gate 4 is exact for `h3_tile_scores`. The softmax, norm and pool kernels state why their output hides the sums' error, as `main`'s softmax and RMS norm do.
- Gate 3 runs at the engine's widths (5,376 and 14,336), and at 2 heads and 16 tiles for the attention and routing kernels.
- The head-layout test keeps the rotary sine small against the cosine. A channel and its partner share one table entry, and a cancelling pair would hide an intermediate rounding from the bound.
- Gates 1–4 ran on GB10; gate 5 covers all five targets.

## Checks

| Check | `main` 46a08c18 | #947 | This branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python3 tools/zig/lean_check.py` | 517 | 517 | 517 |
| `zig build test` (fresh cache) | 84/84 steps, 1376 passed, 7 skipped | 86/86, 1378 passed, 7 skipped | 86/86 steps, 1378 of 1385 passed, 7 skipped, 0 failed |
| `zig build test-kernel-contract` | 18/18 | 18/18 | 18/18 |
| `zig fmt --check`, changed Zig files | | | clean |
| Files ≤ 600 lines | | | largest 324 |

## Gaps and next steps

- **An FP64 reference per projection class.** The products are upstream's `Linear`, unchanged. Its one change of use is a fixed algorithm per shape. This change checks them end to end against the fp32 forward, not class by class in FP64. I can add a per-class FP64 check of q/k/v, out, fc1 and fc2 on the engine's own rows if you want it in this PR.
- **One-GPU speed.** The products are about 73% of a pass and already near the GB10's bf16 rate. The attention (1.47 s) and the head layout (0.48 s, 255 registers) have room left.
- **The exchange.** bf16 doubles the bytes. Overlapping the exchange with the next block's norm and products would hide most of the 1.0 s a 3-rank pass spends in it.
- **How a denoiser fits the engine.** This is unchanged from #947, and it is the same question as #949's.
- **Not yet tested:**
  - GPUs other than GB10;
  - checkpoints other than FastH3 8-Step V2;
  - sizes other than 864x480;
  - four or more ranks;
  - recovery when a rank dies (today the pass fails).

## Licenses

The code is Apache-2.0. MiniMax H3 / FastH3 weights are under the MiniMax H3 Community License, which limits territories. No weights are included.

items.title: music3: MiniMax Music 3 lyrics to song on one CUDA GPU, from Zig (new family; proposal)
items.body:
**Thank you, Ash, for the invitation in #941, and for the CUDA runtime and kernel contract this builds on.**

**This is the first music model on TensorFold's Zig runtime.** MiniMax Music 3 turns a caption and lyrics into a full song with vocals. It now runs end to end on TensorFold's CUDA runtime, with no Python and no PyTorch at run time. It reads Comfy-Org's single-file checkpoints as they are and has its own kernels.

The model has three parts:
- an 8B autoregressive LM with a depth decoder, which writes 8 audio codes a frame at 25 frames a second;
- a 2.4B flow-matching DiT;
- the DAV waveform decoder.

On one DGX Spark (GB10), for a 60 s song:
- **123.9 s with int8 weights, against 289 s for ComfyUI's native nodes on the same GPU.** That is 2.3x faster.
- **17.9 GB peak, against 29.3 GB.**
- **The AR runs at its measured read ceiling:** 20.4 frames/s int8 and 10.4 bf16, against ceilings of 20.7 and 10.4.
- **Parity with ComfyUI at every stage:** code-0 logits cos 0.999977, DiT final latent 37.6 dB, DAV 71 dB (bf16).
- **Kernel contract:** 16 of 16 kernels pass gates 1–4 (the 4 new music3 ones among them), 5 controls red as planted, 0 limit problems.
- **Lean check:** 0 new findings.

I did not open an issue first, since this came by invitation in #941. Happy to move the gate discussion into one if you prefer. It stands alone on `main`: it does not depend on the Drama 3 pull requests.

## Receipts

All on one GB10 (sm_121, 128 GB), idle, one model process, CUDA 13. The checkpoint is Comfy-Org's MiniMax-Music3 repack (`minimax_music3_text_encoder_pruned_bf16`, `minimax_music3_dit_fp16`, `minimax_music3_dav`). The baseline and reference is ComfyUI 5a665890's native nodes on the same machine. The full tables and their JSON are in `docs/recipes/minimax-music3-cuda.md` and `docs/recipes/minimax-music3-cuda/`.

### Measured ceilings before building

Measured on an idle GB10, with weights rotated through a 2 GB pool so L2 never holds them:

| Measurement | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Plain read | 230 GB/s |
| Warp-a-row GEMV, two activation rows, bf16 and int8 | 220–240 GB/s |
| cuBLAS fp16 GEMM, fp32 accumulation, at the DiT's shapes | 96–104 TFLOP/s |
| AR ceiling from those reads | 10.4 frames/s bf16, 20.7 frames/s int8 |
| **AR reached** | **10.4 frames/s bf16, 20.4 frames/s int8** |

What got there:
- **CFG rows share weight reads:** the conditional and unconditional rows go through each GEMV together.
- **The whole frame step is one CUDA graph:** the lm_head, the CFG top-k draw on the device, the depth decoder's 7 passes, and the frame fed back through 36 layers. The host reads the drawn codes every 16 frames for the stop code.
- **PDL:** each GEMV's first weight loads are in flight before `griddepcontrol.wait`.
- **Fused SwiGLU GEMV:** gate and up write the SwiGLU directly.
- **Our own tensor-core flash attention for the DiT,** with rope applied as q and k load (`mma.sync` m16n8k16). There is no `flex_attention`, which gives wrong results on sm_121.
- **Timed cuBLASLt algorithms:** each DiT GEMM shape's algorithm is timed once at load.
- **Bias moved out of the GEMM epilogue,** into the GLU and the next LayerNorm. The bias + accumulate epilogue picked 14 TFLOP/s kernels at some shapes.

### Parity against ComfyUI

Same 30 s input (hiphop bench prompt, seed 7), teacher-forced so the rows are comparable:

| Check | bf16 | int8 (default) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prompt ids | equal (and 10 of 10 id cases) | equal |
| Frame states cos, mean / min | 0.999956 / 0.999556 | 0.999827 / 0.998345 |
| **Code-0 logits cos** | **0.999977** | **0.999897** |
| **Code-0 greedy agreement** | **97.5%** | **96.7%** |
| ComfyUI's drawn code, median rank in ours | 1 | 1 |
| Depth logits cos, codebooks 1–7 | 0.999957–0.999966 | 0.99978–0.99984 |
| DiT probes cos, sigma 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.1 | ≥ 0.999958 | (DiT is fp16 in both) |
| **DiT final latent** (ComfyUI's noise and states) | **cos 0.999914, 37.6 dB** | |
| **DAV of ComfyUI's latent**, chunked as served | **cos 1.0000000, 71.0 dB** | |

The draws themselves cannot match (torch's multinomial against our Philox inverse-CDF draw), so a song is not ComfyUI's song for the same seed, only the same model.

### Speed and memory

Hiphop bench prompt, seed 7, and the long-pop prompt, seed 5, for the 120 s row. Load (37 s from a cold page cache) is outside "total". Peak machine is MemTotal − MemAvailable sampled twice a second, minus the idle machine.

| Song | Weights | AR s (frames/s) | DiT s | DAV s | **Total s** | RTF | Peak machine GB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30 s | int8 | 36.4 (20.9) | 22.0 | 1.9 | **60.3** | 2.01 | 16.6 |
| 60 s | int8 | 73.9 (20.4) | 46.4 | 3.6 | **123.9** | 2.07 | 17.9 |
| 120 s | int8 | 151.7 (19.9) | 93.0 | 7.3 | **252.0** | 2.10 | 19.3 |
| 30 s | bf16 | 72.1 (10.5) | 21.9 | 1.9 | **96.0** | 3.20 | 24.0 |
| 60 s | bf16 | 144.4 (10.4) | 46.3 | 3.6 | **194.3** | 3.24 | 25.5 |
| 120 s | bf16 | 292.7 (10.3) | 93.1 | 7.3 | **393.1** | 3.28 | 26.6 |
| 60 s | ComfyUI baseline | 176 (~9) | 96 | 4 | **289** | 4.8 | 29.3 |

int8 is the default:
- It halves the bytes each frame reads.
- Its parity is within a few 1e-4 of bf16, and ComfyUI's drawn code is rank 1 in both.
- Its lyric accuracy is no lower than bf16's on three songs.

`--weights bf16` reads the checkpoint's own numbers.

### Lyric accuracy

Three 45 s songs, each in bf16 and int8, plus ComfyUI's own 60 s song. Transcribed by faster-whisper large-v3-turbo on the CPU and scored against the lyrics by `tools/music3/lyrics_check.py`. The score counts the words heard up to the last lyric word heard. The span counts only matched runs of 3 or more words.

| Song | bf16 score / span | int8 score / span | Words heard, bf16 / int8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hiphop, seed 7 | 96 / 96 | 98 / 98 | 130 of 135 / 127 of 130 |
| pop, seed 11 | 100 / 100 | 100 / 100 | 78 of 78 / 59 of 59 |
| long-pop, seed 5 | 90 / 89 | 31 / 100 | 50 of 56 / 52 of 52 |
| ComfyUI hiphop 60 s (reference) | 96 / 96 | | 159 of 166 |

The int8 long-pop score of 31 is a scoring artefact: a stray "down" matched the bridge's "go down". Its span is 100.

### Checks on this branch

Run on a GB10 at this head, against `main` 6ee828c2:

- `zig build test`: 86/86 steps; 450/456 tests passed, 6 skipped (libjpeg-turbo absent: JPEG cases).
- `zig build test-cuda-host`: 41/41 steps; 856/856 tests passed (`main`: 852/852).
- Plain `zig build`: succeeded.
- `zig fmt --check zig build.zig`: clean.
- `python3 tools/zig/lean_check.py`: 517 problems, the same 517 as `main`. 0 new findings; the inherited ones are unchanged.
- **Kernel contract** (`zig build kernel-contract -Dnvcc=/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`) on sm_121:

  ```
  SUMMARY 16 kernels: 16 pass gates 1-4, 0 fail, 0 known findings; 5 controls: 5 red as planted, 0 missed; 0 limit problems
  ```

- **Launch limits** (`zig build fatbins kernel-contract-fatbins -Dsm=80,86,89,120,121`, then `tf-cuda-test kernel-contract-limits zig-out/fatbin`):

  ```
  PASS kernel-contract-limits: every registered launch fits sm_80, sm_86, sm_89, sm_120 and sm_121, every control red
  ```

  All 55 music3 launches are registered in `registry.zig` with records for sm_80, sm_86, sm_89, sm_120 and sm_121. `m3_rmsnorm`, `m3_gemv_bf16_2`, `m3_gemv_i8_2` and `m3_gemv_g8_2` go through gates 1–4 (`zig/tests/cuda/contract_music3.zig`).

## What it adds

These are new files, plus the minimal wiring: 11 lines in `zig/build/cuda.zig`, 1 in `zig/src/cuda/kernels.zig`, 12 in the contract runner, 55 records in `registry.zig`, and 1 row in the recipe index.

- **`zig/src/families/music3/`** (Zig over the CUDA runtime):
  - `config.zig` holds the shapes, request settings and the reference's schedules.
  - `prompt.zig` builds the caption and lyrics prompt ids through the core tokenizer and the checkpoint's own `tokenizer_json`.
  - `weights.zig` reads the three files and quantizes int8 on the GPU at load: body and lm_head one scale a row, the depth decoder one scale a group of 128.
  - `ar.zig` holds the AR prompt pass (cuBLAS bf16 GEMMs) and the graphed frame step.
  - `dit.zig` holds the windowed DiT: 689 latent rows every 344, both CFG branches in one forward, on cuBLASLt fp16 GEMMs.
  - `dav.zig` holds the DAV: fp32, every conv as one SGEMM a tap, with no TF32.
  - `engine.zig` and `generate.zig` provide the request, the CLI and `--serve`.
  - `parity.zig` and `npy.zig` provide the parity dumps.
  - `lt.zig` and `blas.zig` open cuBLASLt and cuBLAS at run time.
  - `wav.zig` writes the WAV.
- **`zig/kernels/cuda/music3.cu`** and its headers (`music3_ar.cuh`, `music3_dit.cuh`, `music3_dav.cuh`, `music3_sample.cuh`, `music3_common.cuh`) build one fatbin.
- **`zig build music3-generate`:**
  - caption and lyrics to a WAV;
  - `--ids` for prompt ids with no GPU;
  - `--parity-ar / --parity-probe / --parity-dit / --parity-dav REF` against a reference dump;
  - `--serve 1`.
- **`tools/music3/`** (development tools, Python):
  - `parity.py` builds the parity table from REF and MINE, with numpy only.
  - `lyrics_check.py` measures lyric accuracy with Whisper.
  - `served_test.py` drives `--serve` through the Studio's client.
- **`docs/recipes/minimax-music3-cuda.md`** is the recipe, with the plan and ceilings written before building, the receipts, and their JSON.

## How it fits the engine, and how it does not

- **Serving.** `--serve 1` reads one JSON request a line on stdin and answers on stderr, with optional progress lines. It is the same protocol as our Mac MLX engine for this model, so one client drives either. It answers one request at a time.
- **Lanes.** As with Drama 3 (#939), a step here is a frame of 8 codes, not one `u32` token, and the song is finished by a DiT and a waveform decoder. So this runs as its own generator beside the lane engine rather than on the lane core. Moving it there needs the same core changes #939 lists: a frame position type or a family hook, per-codebook sampling, and an audio output. Plain decoding only; there is no drafter.
- **Native, but not yet one engine request.** Nothing at run time needs Python, PyTorch or ComfyUI. ComfyUI is only the reference for the parity receipts.

## Licences

- **The code** is written for TensorFold and is Apache-2.0. No ComfyUI source is copied in, and nothing here imports ComfyUI. ComfyUI's implementation (GPL-3) is the reference it was checked against. Some parts were written by hand to behave as ComfyUI does, so the outputs line up, and I am naming them so you can decide:
  - the prompt formatting rules;
  - the "simple" sigma schedule;
  - the fp16 rounding of the DiT's rope angles;
  - the top-k tie rule;
  - the DAV level rule.
- **The reference harness is not included.** It is a ComfyUI custom node that records tensors from ComfyUI's own loaders and sampler. The recipe describes what it records and the file layout `parity.py` reads.
- **The model:** MiniMax-Music3 is under the MiniMax-Music3 Community License. No weights are included.
  - A commercial product must display "MiniMax-Music3".
  - Use by a business above $20M a year in revenue needs MiniMax's written authorization.
  - A hosted service must keep the licence's safeguards.

  `music3-generate` prints the display notice, and `--serve` reports `"license_display":"MiniMax-Music3"`.

## Not tested

- GPUs other than GB10. The kernels build and pass gate 5 for sm_80/86/89/120, but nothing ran there. PDL is used only on sm_90 and up.
- fp8, int4 or NVFP4 weights, and fp8 DiT GEMMs.
- Songs over 120 s. The cap is 360 s and the caches are sized for it, but that length was not run.
- Prompts near 5,000 tokens, an instrumental-only lyric check, and non-ASCII section tags.
- Listening by ear beyond spot checks. Lyric accuracy is measured by Whisper.
- Two requests at once: the server answers one at a time.
- The kernel contract covers 4 of the 55 launches through gates 1–4. The rest have gate 5 records only.

## Next steps, if you want them

- **The other launches through gates 1–4,** and the lane-core questions above, for the gate we agree on.
- **A native Metal Music 3 family on the Zig runtime.** Our MLX engine for this model (branch `music3-mlx` on our fork) is a working reference and baseline for it. On an M5 Ultra it does a 60 s song at about real time in int8, with the same parity tables against ComfyUI on MPS. It is Python/MLX, so I have not sent it here: CONTRIBUTING keeps the Python engine frozen at 0.6.6, and the final native request should not need Python.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA (0.6.1 port): the lone stream's graph slot keeps its rows, so its graphs are captured once
items.body:
On the 0.6.1 port, every resize of the lone stream's graph slot drops its graphs: `_grow` and `_shrink` call
`_state_changed`. The slot starts at 256 rows, grows to 8,192 once a reply's context passes them, and shrinks back when
the request ends. So every lone request recaptures its graphs mid-reply: 23 captures, 3.0 s of a 512-token reply on a
GB10. Two and four streams lose 8–11 % the same way, because the first stream starts alone in the slot.

- The slot keeps its rows when idle. It gives them back only when memory is short: an evicted kept end, the newest
  stream ending, or an idle slot freed for another stream's growth.
- It grows by doubling (at least `STEP` rows), so a long session recaptures a handful of times rather than every request.
- `warm()` captures its graphs last. Before, the warm request grew the slot after the captures, which discarded them.
- A different lone request takes the slot without dropping its graphs. A finished request's prompt end is kept in the
  slot it ran in, so the next lone request with another prompt landed elsewhere, and `_move_to_solo` made that slot the
  graph slot (`_state_changed`, a full recapture each request). Now the kept prompt end moves to a free slot of the same
  rows (`copy_from`; its snapshot is unchanged). With no free slot that fits without evicting, the old swap stays.
- `copy_from` takes a source with fewer rows into its first rows, because the graph slot now keeps more rows than a
  stream moving in may have. Rows past `pos` are written before they are read. A larger source is refused.

Two ranks: rank 0 plans on `Shadow`s of the slots, `dec.solo.st` included, so `_is_solo` compares the slots the
Shadows stand for. Keeping the rows records only a reset for rank 1, and a release records the resize like any other.
(The first commit compared a Shadow with the real slot and never matched while planning, so it did nothing on two ranks.
BHCC2025's two-rank run showed it. Fixed in the second commit.) Two ranks keep the slot swap for kept prompt ends,
because the plan names kept ends by slot.

## Measured

One GB10, Flash Next EXL3 3.05bpw, greedy, 512 tokens of code per stream, two starts each:

| | 0.6.0 | `cb5101d` | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--parallel 4`, one request (ms/token) | 13.63 / 13.52 | 18.41 / 18.56 | **12.18 / 12.20** |
| `--parallel 1` (ms/token) | 12.09 / 12.19 | 12.33 / 12.15 | 12.18 / 12.19 |
| two streams (tok/s) | 111.9 / 111.5 | 99.8 / 99.1 | 111.7 / 110.8 |
| four streams (tok/s) | 158.4 / 157.9 | 146.8 / 145.1 | 157.6 / 157.8 |
| graph captures inside the reply (one / two streams) | — | 23 / 8 | 0 / 0 |

Every reply is byte-identical in all three columns.

Lone requests one after another with different prompts (`--parallel 4`, 256 tokens each; the last request resumes the
first one's kept prompt end):

| | `cb5101d` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| graph captures per request | 33 / 32 / 30 / 19 | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 |
| ms/token | 31.6 / 29.4 / 27.3 / 23.0 | 14.0 / 12.7 / 11.7 / 12.1 |

The replies are byte-identical, including the resumed one.

## Tests

`tests/test_cuda_growing_caches.py`:
- The new test checks that the slot keeps its rows across a request's end and gives them to another stream when the
  gate is short. It also checks that the slot grows 8,192 → 16,384 → 32,768 → the window.
- A second test drives the slot through a `Shadow` while planning: it is recognised, keeping its rows records only a
  reset, and a release records the resize. It fails on the first commit.
- The file's decoder helper now sets the port's new attributes (`solo`, `solo_on`, `planning`). Its three existing
  decoder tests failed on `cb5101d` with `AttributeError: ... 'solo'` and pass again.
- Two more tests (third commit): a lone stream moves into a graph slot with more rows (no resize, rows and positions
  carried), and a different lone request takes the graph slot while the kept prompt end moves to a free slot with its
  rows. Both fail on the second commit (a size mismatch in `copy_from`; the slot swapped).
- The file passes 10 of 10. Fourth commit (by @plotarmordev): `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_tp_multi.py`'s lone-stream test
  asserts the new behaviour (the graph slot and its graphs kept, the first prompt's kept end moved, not evicted).
  With it, `test_cuda_growing_caches.py` and `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_{tp_multi,multi,tp,prompt_cache,kvquant}.py`
  give 180 passed, 1 skipped on one GB10 here (178 / 3 on theirs). `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_multi.py` passes 27 of 27 on this PR and on `cb5101d`.

I ran the 14 multi-decoder host test files on both commits. This PR fails 29, `cb5101d` fails 32, and the 29 are a
subset of the 32 (211 pass here). The remainder fail on this machine for other reasons (mostly `mlx` not installed).

Not covered: int8/int4 KV, a two-rank run of the second and third commits (one GPU here), and a server under memory pressure with
the slot holding its rows.

Written with AI assistance (Claude Code); the author reviewed every change.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: refuse quantized bytes where the loader reads bf16 values
items.body:
Two places in the Flash Next NVFP4/ModelOpt loader turn a weight into bf16 by casting, whatever it holds:

- [`weight_bf16`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/c4646171139ee8a3c38103eaa1699dad226ec12b/src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/weights.py#L190-L196) dequantizes block FP8 and casts
  everything else (I wrote that cast in #126). An MXFP8 or per-tensor FP8 `lm_head` would load as raw e4m3 values.
- [`dense()`](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/blob/c4646171139ee8a3c38103eaa1699dad226ec12b/src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/weights.py#L78-L97) returns a weight without a scale as a bf16
  linear, so packed NVFP4 bytes (`uint8`) on a non-expert layer would load as numbers.

Either way the shapes are right, nothing fails, and the model decodes fluent garbage. We hit exactly that on vLLM
with FP8_PB_WO layers read as BF16, and it took a while to see, so a loud refusal is worth a few lines. The checkpoint check
also accepts `NVFP4`/`W4A16_NVFP4` on any layer, and published exports do put it elsewhere:
`myllmbox/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-hibrid48` lists 436 `W4A16_NVFP4` layers, among them the DeltaNet projections and the
head.

## The change

- `_plain(name, w)` in `cuda/weights.py`: a weight a bf16 linear takes must be bf16, fp16 or fp32, else a
  `ValueError` naming the layer and its dtype. `weight_bf16` and `dense()`'s no-scale branch go through it.
- `qwen4_exp.check`: `NVFP4` / `W4A16_NVFP4` outside the routed experts is refused before any weight is read, with
  the first such layer named.

Every supported checkpoint passes: the gate only refuses NVFP4 on layers whose name has no `experts` part, and ours
(`MIXED_PRECISION`: NVFP4 `...mlp.experts`, FP8_PB_WO elsewhere) and the published NVFP4 configs list NVFP4 on
`mlp.experts` only.

## Tests

`tests/test_flashnext_plain_weights.py` (bf16/fp16/fp32 pass, uint8/int8/e4m3 refused) and a case in
`tests/test_hub_and_checks.py` (W4A16 NVFP4 on `linear_attn.in_proj_qkv` refused by name). CPU suite: the same
failures as main on this machine (missing MLX and similar), none new.

Written with AI assistance (Claude Code); the author reviewed every change.

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: keep a state at the last 2048-row boundary before a system block's end, so a block with a new date line resumes there
items.body:
Agent clients put a long system block first and change a few lines near its end on every session: the date line, a memory section. Flash Next on CUDA keeps a state only at the block's end (the second message's start), so a new date makes the whole ~13K-token block prefill again. This PR keeps one more state: the last multiple of 2048 rows at least `MIN_GAP` (256) before the block's end. A block whose second message starts at 13,124 (or anywhere from 12,544 to 14,591) keeps a state at 12,288, and a block that differs only after that resumes there.

On one GB10 with the 4.05 EXL3 pack and `--parallel 4`, a ~13.3K-token block with a new date line went from 18.63-18.79 s to 1.58-1.59 s to first token, with the same tokens.

**What it changes.**
- `cuda/markers.py`: `snapshot_points(openers, assistant, checkpoint=0)` adds the checkpoint to the points when `checkpoint` is set, and exposes it as `points.checkpoint(ids)`. `checkpoint_rows()` reads `TF_SYS_CHECKPOINT` (rows; default 2048, one prompt pass; `0` turns it off; values under `MIN_GAP` are refused).
- `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/engine.py`: Flash Next passes `checkpoint_rows()` to `resume_points`. The other families pass nothing, so their points don't change.
- Nothing else. The checkpoint is one more stop of the existing points: the prompt pass stops there, the fill path snapshots it and `remember`s it, and `slot_for` resumes or forks it like the message-start state. It is evicted in the same order and counts against the same `KEEP`, so the kept-snapshot memory in `indexed_stream_geometry` (`keep + streams`) is unchanged.
- Cost: a prompt that opens with a system block of at least 2304 tokens gets one more prompt-pass stop. With 2048-row passes that land on 2048-row boundaries, the checkpoint usually falls on a boundary that is already there.
- One side effect: a conversation that keeps the checkpoint holds one more of the `KEEP` (8) states, so it can push out an older state one turn sooner.

**Where this comes from.** We run it on our own build (v0.6.4/v0.6.5 plus local patches; see #315, #317). Our version also keeps checkpoints outside our larger kept-state limit and caps them at 4, because our eviction order differs from stock. This PR is the part that stands alone on stock v0.6.5. All the numbers below are from stock v0.6.5 against v0.6.5 plus this PR, with no local patches.

**Environment.**
- One DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121), driver 580.178.04, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1, CUDA 13.0.
- `turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3` `4.05bpw_h6_ng6` at revision `55a732e`, with its stock MTP head. No `TF_*` variables.
- Builds: stock v0.6.5 (`609ca41`) against v0.6.5 plus this PR (`b4a9993`).
- Server: `tensorfold serve <ckpt> --parallel 4 --context 131072 --kv-dtype int8`, the same on both. Each arm booted with the n-gram file's page cache dropped. Arms alternated stock, PR, PR, stock.

**The scenario.**
- A system block of 13,236 tokens in all: a 12.5K-token fixed part (TensorFold's own v0.6.5 docs), then a ~550-token tail with `Conversation started: <date>` and a memory section (the end of the same docs).
- Sessions A, B and C, one after the other, each with its own date. Each asks the same short question (64 tokens, sampled with a fixed seed, thinking off).
- Then B and A again with `"draft": false`. That path takes no kept state, so it is a fresh prefill.

| | A: cached / TTFT | B: cached / TTFT | C: cached / TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock, run 1 | 0 / 18.826 s | 0 / 18.788 s | 0 / 18.793 s |
| this PR, run 1 | 0 / 18.699 s | **12,288 / 1.580 s** | **12,288 / 1.588 s** |
| this PR, run 2 | 0 / 18.714 s | **12,288 / 1.576 s** | **12,288 / 1.592 s** |
| stock, run 2 | 0 / 18.763 s | 0 / 18.660 s | 0 / 18.628 s |

- B and C: TTFT -91.6% (B) and -91.5% (C), the mean of two arms each way. They prefill 948 tokens instead of 13,236.
- A is the first block in each arm, so nothing is kept yet: 18.826 and 18.763 s on stock, 18.699 and 18.714 s with this PR. The extra stop at 12,288 lands on a 2048-row pass boundary, so it costs nothing measurable here.
- The `"draft": false` repeats prefill the whole block in both builds: 18.068-18.242 s.

**Exactness.**
- The scenario's `token_sha`: B and C resumed from the checkpoint against B with `"draft": false` (a fresh prefill): equal in all four arms (B: `59547c01f08c`). A against A with `"draft": false`: equal in all four arms (`615897add3bb`). The same 5 hashes in every arm (C: `9815474d67c1`).
- `bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial --levels 1,2 --tokens 128 --reps 2`:
  - this PR: concurrent against alone 24 / 0 / 0 equal / unequal / failed in each of its two arms; alone against `"draft": false` 12 / 0 / 0 in each;
  - stock: 24 / 0 / 0 and 12 / 0 / 0 in each of its two arms.
- Every reply the servers finished, as `token_sha` from the server's `done` lines: the same multiset of 75 hashes in all four arms (the scenario, `bench_openai`, `bench_concurrent` and `prefill_cold`).

**Decode speed.** `bench_openai.py`, decode tok/s (median of 5) per arm; the change compares the means of the two arms each way:

| prompt, temperature | stock, run 1 | this PR, run 1 | this PR, run 2 | stock, run 2 | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fibonacci-raw, 0.0 | 79.2 | 77.9 | 78.1 | 78.5 | -1.1% |
| fibonacci-raw, 1.0 | 63.8 | 64.3 | 64.3 | 64.5 | +0.2% |
| gpu-chat-no-think, 0.0 | 54.0 | 54.1 | 54.1 | 54.2 | +0.0% |
| gpu-chat-no-think, 1.0 | 49.5 | 50.0 | 52.2 | 52.5 | +0.2% |

`bench_concurrent` aggregate tok/s per arm (same order):

| prompt, temperature, streams | stock, run 1 | this PR, run 1 | this PR, run 2 | stock, run 2 | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| code, 0.0, 1 | 89.5 | 89.4 | 89.4 | 89.6 | -0.2% |
| code, 0.0, 2 | 151.1 | 151.7 | 151.5 | 151.2 | +0.3% |
| chat, 0.0, 1 | 56.5 | 56.6 | 56.6 | 56.8 | -0.1% |
| chat, 0.0, 2 | 95.9 | 95.8 | 96.1 | 96.6 | -0.3% |
| code, 1.0, 1 | 87.8 | 87.9 | 87.8 | 88.2 | -0.2% |
| code, 1.0, 2 | 88.0 | 104.5 | 104.3 | 105.2 | +8.1% |
| chat, 1.0, 1 | 53.0 | 53.6 | 53.6 | 53.8 | +0.4% |
| chat, 1.0, 2 | 73.0 | 71.7 | 73.9 | 74.0 | -1.0% |

Sampled code at two streams was 88.0 in the first stock arm and 104.3-105.2 in the other three, so that +8.1% is a slow first arm, not this PR. No decode path changes: these prompts have no system block, so they get no checkpoint. The -1.1% `bench_openai` row is the same greedy decode that `bench_concurrent` measures at -0.2% with one stream.

**Prompt speed.** `prefill_cold.py run` on a trimmed set (2K ×2, 8K ×2, 16K ×1; one 1K warm-up), median TTFT in seconds per arm:

| prompt tokens | stock, run 1 | this PR, run 1 | this PR, run 2 | stock, run 2 | change |
