items.title: feat(flash next cuda): --parallel N on two ranks
items.body:
Follows up #123. Flash Next with `--tp 2` served one request at a time and refused `--parallel`. This lets both ranks share each round between several requests. Measured with your `tools/bench_concurrent.py`, 8 users get 2.4-3.4x the total throughput and every reply keeps its solo run's token ids. A single request under `--parallel` gives up 2-4%, which we left as is (details below).

## What changes

- **Rank 0 plans, rank 1 runs that plan.** Only rank 0 schedules. It sends rank 1 each admission, round, completion and drop, in the order it runs them, over one TCP connection. The connection uses `TCP_NODELAY`, and its ephemeral port on the `--master` address is published through the rendezvous store. An admission carries the slot rank 0 chose and the kept prompt end it resumes from, and rank 1 takes exactly those instead of choosing.
- **The ranks can't drift apart unnoticed, and neither is left waiting.** Before each admission and each round, both ranks confirm the plan in one small all-gather. For an admission that's the stream, slot, resume point, prompt and sampling. For a round it's the live streams, their lengths, drafts and slots. If the plans ever differ, both ranks raise `OutOfStep` at the same point, before any of that step's collectives. The requests in that step fail with the error and serving goes on. Checking over the socket alone would have left rank 0 inside NCCL, which has no timeout, if rank 1 stopped. At startup both ranks must also agree on `--parallel`, beside the settings already checked.
- **A request that ends on rank 0 alone** (the client left) is named in the next round message, so rank 1 ends it too before the check. It is then finished on both ranks as usual.
- **Sampling over the split vocabulary per stream.** `choose_gathered_streams` picks every stream's tokens from the step's gathered candidates with one read-back. A rule wider than the gathered candidates goes through `tp_sample_rows`, and drafts do the same (`_picks_tp`).
- **A lone stream replays the one-stream CUDA graphs**, as #84 does for Qwen3.6. The graphs' `State` is one of the slots. A stream left decoding alone moves into it with `State.copy_from`, which copies in place and keeps the captured addresses. This helps one GPU as well.
- **Admission:** `indexed_stream_geometry(world=...)`. The graphs' buffers are counted as one more stream, which is generous.
- **Structured output under `--tp 2 --parallel` is refused with an HTTP 400 before anything is generated.** The message says why and what to do instead, and the startup line says so too. Images were already refused because Flash Next on CUDA is text-only. One GPU, and two ranks without `--parallel`, are unchanged.

## The checks you listed

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| Rank 0 plans each round and rank 1 runs the same plan | `follow` runs rank 0's ops in order, with rank 0's slot and resume point. `test_tp_rank_1_takes_rank_0s_slot_and_resume_point_or_both_refuse_the_admission` and `test_tp_ranks_planning_a_different_round_both_refuse_it_and_serve_on` put rank 1 out of step on purpose: both ranks refuse that step, the request gets `OutOfStep`, the next request is exact, and every slot on rank 1 is free at the end |
| Every reply equals its `"draft": false` run and its solo run by token ids at 1, 2, 4 and 8 users | `test_tp_every_reply_equals_its_serial_run_and_its_solo_run_at_1_2_4_8_users`, greedy and 7 sampling rules mixed; on two Sparks, below |
| A resumed prompt equals a fresh one | `test_tp_a_resumed_prompt_equals_the_same_prompt_fresh` (same prompt resumed from a kept slot, fresh on a new decoder, and serial); on two Sparks, below |
| A cancel or disconnect during prefill or decode leaves neither rank hanging | `test_tp_a_client_leaving_in_prefill_or_decode_leaves_neither_rank_hanging` through the real `Scheduler`, and `test_tp_a_stream_rank_0_ends_at_its_first_token_...`, which failed with "out of step" before the round-message change above; both assert every slot free on rank 1 at the end |
| Structured output and images refused, not served one at a time | `test_an_engine_refusing_structured_output_says_why_before_generating`; on two Sparks, below |

## Evidence

**Measured with your concurrency bench, `tools/bench_concurrent.py`**, as docs/recipes/README.md describes: `--levels 1,2,4,8 --alone --serial --reps 3` (256 tokens, `ignore_eos`), unchanged from 0.5.0. Setup: two DGX Sparks, Qwen3.8 Flash Next MLX 4-bit, `--tp 2 --context 65536`, int8 KV. We compared 0.5.0 without `--parallel` against this branch with `--parallel 8`. Figures are aggregate tok/s, 0.5.0 → this PR, medians of 3:

| Users | code greedy | code sampled | chat greedy | chat sampled |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 107.1 → 104.9 | 105.6 → 101.4 | 86.0 → 83.9 | 84.0 → 80.7 |
| 2 | 104.5 → 173.2 | 97.1 → 126.5 | 85.2 → 139.7 | 85.8 → 113.3 |
| 4 | 103.8 → 258.5 | 101.4 → 171.8 | 84.4 → 209.2 | 82.1 → 146.8 |
| 8 | 103.6 → 345.4 | 101.9 → 223.7 | 84.0 → 283.8 | 78.7 → 185.5 |

The tool's own checks passed in every cell on both versions. Each concurrent reply had the same token ids as its solo run: 45/45 in each of the 4 cells, 180 in all. Each solo run matched `"draft": false`.

**A single request is 2-4% slower than 0.5.0** when the server runs with `--parallel`, going through the lone-stream path: 104.9 against 107.1 tok/s for code greedy, and 80.7 against 84.0 for chat sampled. We did not try to close that gap in this PR. Our own 512-token greedy run agrees, at about 107.5 against 111 tok/s. Serving without `--parallel` is unchanged. Happy to look into it separately if it matters to you. On one Spark, a lone stream ran at 81.4 tok/s against 81.9 before, and two streams ran 19% faster.

Our own end-to-end checks on the two Sparks, beside your bench. Each reply was compared **by token ids**, using the `token_sha` every reply carries in `tensorfold`, with the same request's `"draft": false` reply on the same server. Its text was also compared with the serial replies recorded on unmodified 0.5.0. The script is `exact3.py`; we can add it under `tools/` if that helps your run.

- 1, 2, 4 and 8 users at once, 8 cases (greedy, and `top_k` 20 and 0, mixed): 15/15 equal to serial by token ids, 15/15 equal to the solo run, and 15/15 equal to 0.5.0's text.
- Resumed against fresh: 6 second turns, each sent first with nothing kept (cached 0), then after its first turn, resuming from 21-29 kept tokens. All 12 equal to serial by token ids. All 6 sent at once: 6/6 equal. Three of them resumed; the other three found their kept slots taken by the requests arriving with them and prefilled fresh.
- Hang-ups, twice over: 2 clients closed 0.4 s into a ~20K-token prefill and 2 mid-reply, beside 4 live requests. The live 8/8 equal by token ids, then 8 at once afterwards 8/8 equal. Neither rank logged an error.
- Our wider suite (`exact2.py`), 16 cases: greedy, `top_k` 20/0/50, `min_p`, `ignore_eos`, stop strings, a 2K-token reply and a ~20K-token prompt. They were run alone, all 16 at once (more than the slots), staggered, mixed with hang-ups and invalid requests, and at once again. All 80 replies and the 4 multi-turn conversations were identical.
- `response_format`, streamed or not, and `guided_regex` gave an HTTP 400 with the reason, in under 10 ms. An image gave a 400 too.

## Checks

- `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_tp_multi.py` is new. It runs two ranks in two threads, as `test_flashnext_tp.py` does, with the same fakes.
- The Flash Next CUDA tests, `tests/test_cuda_response_format.py` and `tests/test_cuda_server*.py` give 342 passed, 18 skipped. The skips are the xgrammar cases, which aren't installed in our container.
- `ruff check` adds no findings on the changed files, compared with `main`.
- Not in this PR: grammar under two-rank `--parallel`. One more thing: a failure inside a step on one rank only, such as running out of memory on one Spark mid-prefill, still leaves the other rank waiting in NCCL, as it does on the serial two-rank path today.

We're happy to rework any of it, for example sending the plan through the store or a collective instead of the socket, if you'd rather.

items.title: perf(flash next cuda): read a prompt pass's n-gram rows before waiting on the previous step's copies
items.body:
**Branch:** `perf/flash-next-stage-ahead` (one commit, da6caed, on `v0.6.0`, c464617)

**TL;DR:** Flash Next's `stage()` waited for the previous step's copies out of the pinned staging buffers, and only then gathered the pass's n-gram (PLE) rows from the memory-mapped table. The GPU idled through that gather after every prompt pass, and longer when table pages had been evicted. The rows are now gathered before the wait and copied into the buffers after it, so the gather overlaps the previous step's GPU work. The same rows reach the same buffers, so prompts, decode and kept states keep their bits.

## The problem

- `stage()` called `b.staged.synchronize()` first. That event is recorded after the previous step's copies out of the pinned buffers. Only then did it gather each layer's n-gram rows (`p.table.gather(ids)`) and copy them in.
- The gather runs on the host and touches pages of the mapped n-gram table, about 27 GiB for the NVFP4 checkpoint. An NVFP4 table is never locked (`NVFP4Table.lock()` returns `False`), and the memory gate counts its pages as reclaimable.
- Once memory fills and the kernel evicts table pages, the gather page-faults, and the GPU waits for all of it after every pass.

## The change

- `stage()` collects the pass's lookups (layer, row ids, first staging row) and gathers the rows for all layers before the wait.
  - After the wait, it writes the token ids and copies the gathered rows into the pinned buffers, as before.
  - `stage_ple_rows` takes the already-gathered rows (`got=`). Without them it gathers them itself, as before.
- EXL3 packs keep their order: `stage_ple` reads into the pinned buffers directly.
- `TF_FLASH_STAGE_AHEAD=0` restores the old order.
- The buffers, copies and rows are the same; only the moment of the gather moves.

## Measurements

Jetson AGX Thor, one container session (`up-u2`). Upstream 0.6.0 plus this commit, `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` rev `7c4f1bc1`, `--kv-dtype int8 --parallel 4`. The engine reads the switch at each `stage()`, so both orders run in one process on the same prompts. Cold prefill wall time, every request counted:

| Prompt | `TF_FLASH_STAGE_AHEAD=0` (before) | this change | Change | Head logits |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| synthetic 8k | 903 tok/s | 923 tok/s | +2.2% | identical |
| synthetic 32k | 889 tok/s | 890 tok/s | +0.1% | identical |
| natural text 32k | 862 tok/s | 868 tok/s | +0.7% | identical |
| **natural text 32k, n-gram table dropped from the page cache** | **773 tok/s** | **857 tok/s** | **+10.8%** | identical |
| synthetic 128k | 789 tok/s | 792 tok/s | +0.4% | identical |
| one-user greedy decode, 512 tokens (median of 3) | 66.55 tok/s | 66.57 tok/s | 0% | identical ids |

The decode row is in-process greedy decode with MTP drafts, not a served-request metric. The first decode with stage-ahead on was 58.11 tok/s. The median drops it. The other five runs are 66.50-66.59 tok/s with the same ids.

The prefill cells are single runs; a gain under about 1% is within run-to-run noise.

The cold row drops the table's pages before the prompt. The log records `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` (`madvise_rc` 0) and resident pages falling to about 0. That is what a long-running server sees once other memory has pushed the table out.

## Tests

- New: `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py::test_stage_reads_the_ngram_rows_ahead_with_the_same_bits`. With the switch on and off, a prompt in passes of 16 and then 5 rows gives the same first token, staged rows, streams and decoded tokens.
- An earlier session on the same code (`up-u1`): `test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py` **26 passed** (including the new test); `test_flashnext_forward.py` plus `test_flashnext_multi.py` **79 passed, 2 failed**. The measurement session (`up-u2`) did not re-run those full files.
  - The 2 failures are `test_flashnext_multi.py::test_packed_passes_keep_each_prompt_one_token_early[bf16]` and `[int8]`. In the measurement session, the same two tests with 0.6.0's `forward.py` failed the same assertion: stream 4's output is `[2033, 2685, 530, 0]` and `serial_decode` continues `[2033, 2685, 530, 0, 979, ...]`.
  - That failure is already present on plain 0.6.0.
- Not run: DGX Spark, CPU tests.

The commit also applies cleanly to the 0.6.1 branch (`pr-141-0.6.1`): `git cherry-pick` merges `forward.py` and the loader test without conflicts. It was not tested there.

items.title: fix(flash next cuda): build the CUDA extensions before the weights load
items.body:
**Branch:** `fix/flash-next-build-before-load` (one commit, 5c5931b, on `v0.6.0`, c464617)

**TL;DR:** On a first start after an install or an update, `tensorfold.cuda.build.load` compiles each CUDA extension the first time a step needs it. Flash Next met them in its prompt warm-up, after the weights had loaded. On a Jetson AGX Thor (unified memory), that left the server with **1.36-2.00 GiB less MemAvailable** than the next start (two sessions), still missing 20 s after the server came up. The engine now loads every extension it uses right after admission, before the weights load. With the same builds, the difference is **0.01-0.15 GiB**, about the 0.1 GiB by which two starts that build nothing differ.

## The problem

- Upstream 0.6.0 with an empty extension cache (a first start after `pip install -U` or `tensorfold update`) builds six extensions: `tensorfold_nvfp4_prompt_v1`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn_io`, `tensorfold_gdn_v2`, `tensorfold_experts_v7`, `tensorfold_nvfp4_v3` and `tensorfold_qmm_v3`. All six are built after the weights load, in the warm-up.
- After such a start, MemAvailable is 1.36-2.00 GiB lower than after the next start, which builds nothing (MemFree moves with it), measured 20 s after the server is up.
- The missing memory is not in the server's resident set (1.88-1.93 GiB on every start). Net `Cached` moved by 0.07 GiB or less, and `AnonHugePages` by 0.14 GiB. In the first stock session, about 1 GiB moved from `Active(file)` to `Inactive(file)` while net `Cached` stayed put. Where the missing GiB is held is not identified.
- Why it matters: on a unified GPU, `MemoryGate.fits` checks the caches' growth against live MemAvailable. So the streams' caches have 1.4-2 GiB less to grow into for as long as the memory stays missing. How long that lasts in a running server was not measured. The printed "free for their caches" does not show it: it reads the same after both starts.

## The change

- New `engine.build_kernels(exl3=, nvfp4=, solo=)`, which loads:
  - for every start: `experts`, `kernels.gdn`, `kernels.qmm` and `qwen4_exp.cuda.gdn_io`;
  - for NVFP4 (ModelOpt) checkpoints: the NVFP4 linears' two extensions;
  - for EXL3 packs: the EXL3 experts' and linears' extensions;
  - for one stream only: `qwen4_exp.cuda.gdn` (concurrent rounds never use it).
- `FlashNextEngine.__init__` calls it right after admission, so a refused start builds nothing, and before `weights.load`.
- On a start with a built cache it only loads the modules.
- Tests:
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py::test_the_engine_loads_its_extensions_before_the_weights`, at one and two streams. It records every `tensorfold.cuda.build.load` call and the `weights.load` call during a start and a first request on the synthetic checkpoint, and checks that no extension is loaded after the weights. It clears the loaders' `lru_cache` first, so each one goes through `build.load`.
  - `tests/test_cuda_capacity.py::fake_runtime`, which stops a start at its weights load to test admission without a GPU, now stubs `build_kernels`.

## Measurements

Jetson AGX Thor, `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` rev `7c4f1bc1`, `--kv-dtype int8 --parallel 4`. Two container sessions (1: `up-m1`, 2: `up-b4`), each with four starts in a row; the server was stopped and given 15 s between starts. MemAvailable was read 20 s after the server answered `/v1/models`:

| Session | Tree | Builds on the first start | MemAvailable after the first start | after the next start (no builds) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.6.0 | 6, after the weights load | 40.99 GiB | 42.99 GiB | **-2.00 GiB** |
| 1 | an earlier revision of this change, which also built the one-stream chain | 7, before the load | 42.87 GiB | 42.88 GiB | -0.01 GiB |
| 2 | 0.6.0 | 6, after the weights load | 41.65 GiB | 43.01 GiB | **-1.36 GiB** |
| 2 | this change | 6, before the load | 42.91 GiB | 43.05 GiB | -0.15 GiB |

- With 0.6.0, MemFree fell with MemAvailable (-1.98 and -1.36 GiB). The server's resident set (1.88-1.93 GiB in every start), anonymous memory, page cache and slab each moved by 0.14 GiB or less.
- Two starts that build nothing differ by up to 0.11 GiB (the two trees' second starts: 42.88 vs 42.99, 43.05 vs 43.01). The -0.15 GiB with this change is close to that.
- The builds take the same time either way: in session 2, the first start was ready after 285 s on 0.6.0 and 290 s with this change, against 86-87 s for a start that builds nothing. These are single runs.
- The printed "free for their caches" reads 32.2-32.3 GiB in all eight starts.
- The measurement is a small shell script around `tensorfold serve` and `/proc/meminfo`.

The same kind of loss showed up earlier on a local Thor branch, on a first start that built its extensions after the weights loaded. Not measured: DGX Spark. It is also unified memory, so it may behave the same way.

## Tests

- **New test:** `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py::test_the_engine_loads_its_extensions_before_the_weights`, at one and two streams.
  - Both pass with this change.
  - With 0.6.0's `engine.py`, both fail. One stream lists `tensorfold_experts_v7`, `tensorfold_qmm_v3`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn_io` and `tensorfold_gdn_v2`. Two streams list the same set without `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn`. The synthetic checkpoint does not load the NVFP4 extensions.
- **On the same Thor, with this change (`up-b4`, `up-b5`):**
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py`: **56 passed**.
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py`, `test_flashnext_tp.py` and `test_flashnext_multi.py`: **70 passed, 2 skipped, 2 failed**. The 2 failures are `test_flashnext_multi.py::test_packed_passes_keep_each_prompt_one_token_early[bf16]` and `[int8]`. They fail the same way on plain 0.6.0 (details in the stage-ahead PR).
  - With no GPU visible, the CPU tests that construct engines up to the weights load (`tests/test_cuda_capacity.py`, `test_cuda_kv_dtype.py`, `test_cuda_parallel_admission.py`, `test_cuda_admission.py`, `test_exl3_engines.py` and `test_cuda_nemotron_admission.py`): **147 passed**.
- **Not run:**
  - an EXL3 pack on a GPU, so the EXL3 loaders in `build_kernels` are exercised only by the CPU tests, which stub it;
  - DGX Spark.

The commit also applies cleanly to the 0.6.1 branch (`pr-141-0.6.1`). There, the list in `build_kernels` should be checked against the vision and image-row paths it adds. The new test would show any extension loaded after the weights.

items.title: feat(cuda): one communicator interface for two-rank engines (transports over NCCL)
items.body:
## What this changes

Two-rank CUDA engines get one place to plug in a faster or different transport. `tensorfold.cuda.comm` gains a small
communicator interface, and the three engines that built `NCCL(rank, 2, master, port)` themselves (GLM-5.3, Flash
Next, Nemotron) open it with `open_comm(rank, 2, master, port)`. With `TF_COMM_BACKEND` unset, nothing changes.

- `Comm`: what every engine may assume (`rank`, `world`, `all_gather`, `barrier`).
- `fast_gather(comm, send, recv)`: the transport's `all_gather_fast` if it has one, else `all_gather`.
- `exchange(comm, sends, recvs, peer=None)`: `NCCL.exchange` (one `ncclSend` / `ncclRecv` group on the current
  stream). Without it, two ranks trade bytes through the all-gather.
- `check(comm)`: raises a failure the transport recorded.
- `Transport`: a base that wraps NCCL and forwards whatever a subclass does not define (`store`, `ready`,
  `all_gather`, and later NCCL methods), so a transport overrides only what it speeds up.
- `register_backend(name, wrap)` / `open_comm(...)`: `TF_COMM_BACKEND` picks a registered transport; unset, it
  builds the same NCCL as `NCCL(...)`. The ranks compare the name through the rendezvous store and refuse to start
  if they differ, since a transport on one rank only would hang the first exchange. An unknown name is refused
  before NCCL is set up.
- `NCCL` gathers `uint8`, `int8` and `float16` too, and takes the rendezvous timeout and store key (defaults
  unchanged: 600 s and `tf_nccl_uid`).

Why: one-shot RoCE all-gathers on DGX Sparks now exist in three places (ours for two-Spark GLM-5.3-Flash, MiaAI-Lab's
`RoceComm`, and the one inside #159), each switched into one engine by its own variable. On our pair a 16 KiB
graph-captured gather takes 11.7 us against NCCL's 45.3 us, and decode gains 4-11% with the same bits. Point-to-point
trades (MiaAI-Lab's `NCCL.exchange`, #159's all-to-all) have the same problem. A transport written once under this
interface can serve any two-rank family. A `roce` transport would be a separate pull request on top of this one.

Rebased onto 0.6.3. `comm.py` and the three call sites had not changed upstream, and no new direct `NCCL(...)`
construction was added (#159 is still open). Qwen3.8-27B's `torch.distributed` process group is not an `NCCL`
object and is left as is. The optional `CUDA_SERVE` commit from the first version was dropped to keep one change in
this pull request; it was the only part that conflicted.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold 0.6.3 (`9356df5`) plus these two commits. Linux x86_64, Python 3.14.7, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu,
  no GPU, no MLX, no Triton. No checkpoint was loaded.
- Exactness: not run. With `TF_COMM_BACKEND` unset, `open_comm` builds the same `NCCL` object with the same
  arguments and the engines make the same exchanges in the same order; the only new step is one store round trip at
  start in which the ranks compare the backend name. The new functions have no caller in the tree yet.
- Decode speed: not run, for the same reason; the decode path is unchanged.
- Prompt speed: not run, for the same reason; no prefill path, kernel or family exchange changes.
- Tests run, with pass, fail and skip counts:
  - `tests/test_cuda_comm.py` (new, 10 tests) and `tests/test_cuda_capacity.py`, with `tests/test_cuda_comm_ready.py`:
    61 passed on this branch. On 0.6.3 with these test files: 27 failed, 34 passed. The 10 comm tests fail because
    the interface does not exist; the 17 two-rank GLM-5.3 and Flash Next capacity tests fail because the stand-in for
    `tensorfold.cuda.comm` now offers only `open_comm`, which 0.6.3's engines do not call.
  - Without PyTorch, the same two files collect and skip cleanly: 12 passed, 37 skipped.
  - Full suite, `python -m pytest -q -n 4 --timeout 300 --continue-on-collection-errors tests`, same session:
    this branch 3,442 passed, 208 skipped, 148 failed, 14 errors; clean 0.6.3 3,432 passed, 208 skipped, 148 failed,
    14 errors. The 162 failing and erroring ids are identical. They are 0.6.3's own on a Linux box without MLX,
    Triton or a GPU (MLX server, prompt fill and reasoning tests).
- Not run, and why: no GPU here, so the CUDA runtime, `tests/cuda`, and the two-rank NCCL start were not run. The GPU
  tests that replace `tensorfold.cuda.comm.NCCL` with a fake (`tests/cuda/test_flashnext_tp.py`,
  `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py`) reach it through `open_comm` unchanged. Nothing was run on Metal; this
  change touches no Metal path. If you want a GPU receipt, I can run `tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial`,
  `tools/bench_openai.py` and `tools/prefill_cold.py` on two DGX Sparks, before and after.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo.
      (Not measured here; the exchanges are the same NCCL calls as before.)
- [x] No precision traded for speed. If the bits change, the description says which sums change and why.

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B CUDA: --kv-dtype int8 (packed -cq 8 rows; drafted rounds -6% at 90k, -13% at 242k)
items.body:
The 27B's CUDA engine can now keep its attention caches in int8 with `--kv-dtype int8` (one GPU). The default stays bf16, and the bf16 path's output is byte-identical to 0.6.1/0.6.2 (checked on fixed inputs, 1 to 128 rows, up to 90k keys).

Why: on a DGX Spark the 27B's decode slows with depth because every round reads the whole bf16 cache (64 KiB a position over the 16 attention layers). Real long agentic sessions here sit at ~100k tokens, where a drafted round costs ~145 ms against ~106 ms at 3k. int8 halves those bytes.

## Design

- **Same scheme as Flash Next's cache**: ExLlamaV3 `-cq 8` (each group of 32 values rotated by a 32-point Hadamard, fp16 absmax scale, midpoint grid). The quantizer is Flash Next's own `kvquant.quant_groups_8`/`dequant_group_8`, so the codes and scales are bit-identical to `kvcache.quantize_ref`.
- **Packed rows** (`tensorfold/cuda/kernels/kvpack.py`): a (position, KV head) row is `head_dim` int8 codes followed by `head_dim/32` fp16 scales (272 bytes at head dim 256). A layer's cache is still one tensor indexed by position, so `grow`, `reserve`, commit copies, clones, kept states and the KV room work unchanged.
- **Drafts equal serial**: a verify window packs its keys and values *before* attention, and the tree attention dequantizes committed rows and the row's own path alike. A drafted row therefore reads exactly what serial decoding reads after a commit, which is now a byte copy of the accepted packed rows.
- **Prompts keep their bits in any chunking**: prefill stores packed rows and attends over the dequantized prefix (`kvpack.unpack`, rotated back to the model's basis). Every key, the chunk's own included, passes through its codes, so a resumed prompt equals a fresh one. The CUDA prefill attention kernel is unchanged.
- The query is rotated once (`kvpack.rotate`) and the merged output rotated back in `_merge`.
- int8 plans hold 32 (row, head) pairs an item (`PACKED_TILE`). With 16, a 16-row window over 24 heads dequantizes each key tile six times and int8 gained nothing over bf16 at 16 rows. 64 pairs spilled registers. 32 with Flash Next's reshape dequant was the fastest of the variants measured on GB10.
- Admission counts the packed bytes plus one layer's dequantized prompt read. The concurrent decoder's memory gate uses the packed row size. `--tp 2` refuses `--kv-dtype int8`.

## Measured on one DGX Spark (GB10)

Two public checkpoints:
- `Vontra/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit`, the docs' standard checkpoint;
- [`armin1/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-FP8-Mixed-LH`](https://huggingface.co/armin1/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-FP8-Mixed-LH), a ModelOpt mixed checkpoint (NVFP4 MLP with the last 8 layers in FP8, FP8 attention/DeltaNet/head), served with `--precision full`.

Both used `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` and `--parallel 3 --thinking --prefill-fp8`, with both cache dtypes in the same build (0.6.2 + this branch). Round time = decode seconds over rounds from `/health` (it separates the cache's cost from acceptance). Prompts are seeded non-repeating log lines plus one 512-token code request, greedy.

ms a drafted round:

| Prompt tokens | MLX 4-bit, bf16 | int8 | NVFP4/FP8 mixed, bf16 | int8 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2,890 | 82.9 | 82.8 | 106.1 | 105.8 |
| 45,100 | 102.2 | 96.3 | 125.4 | 120.5 |
| 90,220 | 121.6 | 113.6 (−7%) | 144.9 | 136.0 (−6%) |
| 180,500 | 159.9 | 144.1 (−10%) | 184.0 | 168.3 (−9%) |
| 242,500 | 188.6 | 164.5 (−13%) | 213.1 | 186.4 (−13%) |

`"draft": false`, ms a token: MLX 4-bit 96.4 → 86.5 at 90k and 143.1 → 114.4 at 242k (−10%, −20%); NVFP4/FP8 mixed 118.4 → 108.3 and 164.3 → 136.5 (−9%, −17%). Prompt fill is within 2% of bf16. The startup estimate at the 262,144 window drops from 37.39 to 30.38 GiB (MLX) and from 43.60 to 36.59 GiB (NVFP4/FP8). Short-context decode is unchanged (code / prose tok/s, bf16 vs int8: MLX 78.8 / 50.2 vs 81.2 / 50.1, NVFP4/FP8 mixed 66.5 / 39.4 vs 66.3 / 38.6).

Tree attention alone (24 q heads / 4 KV heads, head dim 256, median of 50), ms a layer:

| Keys | 16 rows bf16 | int8 | 1 row bf16 | int8 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2,048 | 0.112 | 0.134 | 0.067 | 0.097 |
| 32,768 | 0.893 | 0.729 | 0.622 | 0.427 |
| 90,000 | 2.336 | 1.839 | 1.713 | 1.125 |
| 131,072 | 3.320 | 2.576 | 2.485 | 1.587 |
| 180,000 | 4.536 | 3.507 | 3.415 | 2.162 |

Quality (100 local tasks, greedy, thinking off, 1,024 tokens; needle at 194,893 tokens):

| Checkpoint, cache | GSM8K | JSON | Code | Instructions | Greedy agreement with BF16 | Needle |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| MLX 4-bit, bf16 | 48/50 | 14/15 | 25/25 | 8/10 | 41.9% | correct |
| MLX 4-bit, int8 | 47/50 | 14/15 | 24/25 | 9/10 | 43.0% | correct |
| NVFP4/FP8 mixed, bf16 | 48/50 | 14/15 | 25/25 | 8/10 | 55.8% | correct |
| NVFP4/FP8 mixed, int8 | 49/50 | 14/15 | 25/25 | 7/10 | 55.2% | correct |

Items change in both directions:
- On NVFP4/FP8 mixed, int8 answers one GSM8K question bf16 misses and misses one instruction task. On both, it gives the unquantized model's result.
- On MLX, int8 runs one GSM8K answer to the token cap and fails one code test.
- On MLX, int8 also passes an instruction task that bf16 and the unquantized model both miss.

The EXL3 path shares the same forward and cache code but was not run end to end here.

## Tests

`tests/cuda/test_qwen27_kv_int8.py` (22 tests):
- packed codes and scales equal `kvcache.quantize_ref` bit for bit;
- `unpack` and `rotate` equal the reference H32;
- branch nodes equal their serial bits with packed caches, from 0 to 20,501 keys;
- streams in one launch equal each alone;
- packed attention matches torch on the dequantized rows;
- bf16/packed mixing and a wrong-tile plan are refused;
- every int8 prefill chunking gives the same state;
- an int8 resume equals fresh, and drafts equal serial;
- the int8 prompt tracks bf16 closely.

`tests/test_cuda_cli.py` now expects the 27B to accept `int8`. GLM still refuses it, and `int4` stays refused for the 27B. On one GB10, the attention, prefill-attention, Flash Next kvquant, all `test_qwen27_*`, CLI, geometry and KV-room suites pass (415 passed, 20 skipped).

## Not in this PR

- `int4` for the 27B.
- Two ranks.
- Fusing the dequant into the CUDA prefill attention kernel. Prompts read a bf16 copy of the prefix, one layer at a time, and admission counts it.
- The fp32 chunk partials that `_shared` writes and `_merge` reads back. They cost int8 and bf16 alike, about 0.6 ms a layer at 90k with 16 rows, and are a separate change.

items.title: feat(flash-next cuda): TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS sets the prompt piece rows
items.body:
**TL;DR:** `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS=N` (256 to 16,384) sets Flash Next's prompt piece rows on CUDA. Unset or empty keeps today's behaviour exactly.

## The problem

Flash Next fills prompts in 2,048-row pieces, or 4,096 while idle on a DGX Spark serving the MLX checkpoint without `--vision` when the admitted window leaves room (`prompt_plan.choose`). Neither suits every deployment: the best piece size depends on the machine and on where the n-gram tables are read from, and an operator could not change it without editing the source.

## The change

- `cuda/geometry.indexed_prefill_rows()` reads `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS`: None when unset or empty, the rows when 256 to 16,384, and a startup refusal for anything else.
- `FlashNextEngine` sizes the startup geometry's prompt buffers for N rows (one GPU or two), so the admitted window matches, and the idle plan no longer applies. A round beside live replies still takes at most 2,048 rows (`prompt_plan.pass_limit`).
- EXL3 packs keep their own buffers and ignore it.
- `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md` describes the pieces and the variable.

Replies are the same tokens at any setting; only prompt speed and the startup estimate change.

## Testing

- `tests/test_flash_next_prefill_rows_env.py`: unset and empty, accepted values, refused values.
- On one DGX Spark (Flash Next MLX 4-bit, `--parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --ple-on-ssd --vision`), `TENSORFOLD_PREFILL_ROWS=3072` starts with "idle prompt pieces 3072 rows".
- The geometry, capacity and Flash Next memory tests pass. `tests/test_flash_next_pass_rows.py` fails the same way on `main` (`MultiDecoder` has no `streams` in its fixture).

items.title: Flash Next CUDA: /v1/decisions scores labels from the prompt's last logits, the questions filling in one pass
items.body:
0.6.1 added `POST /v1/decisions`, but on CUDA it needs the engine's `score_labels`, which Flash Next does not have:
`this model's CUDA engine does not score decision labels`. This adds it, on one GPU.

## What changes

- **`FlashNextEngine.score_labels` / `score_labels_many`** (`families/qwen4_exp/cuda/engine.py`): a one-token greedy request with `draft=False`, whose collector reads the label logits and the full-vocabulary logsumexp at the prompt's last position. `draft=False` means the decision neither resumes from nor leaves a kept prompt state, so decisions never evict a conversation's kept end (that table is only 8 entries). One GPU only, like logprobs (`supports_logprobs`).
- **`LabelProbabilities`** (`engine/probabilities.py`) and **`capture`** (`cuda/logprobs.py`): when the collector carries `labels`, `capture` also gathers those columns of the row it already reduces; nothing else changes for logprobs.
- **`Scheduler.submit_many`** (`cuda/scheduler.py`): queues several one-shot requests from one thread. Submitted one by one from threads, the first woke the worker, which filled it alone; queued together they fill in one pass (`ENDS = 16`).
- **The decisions route** (`cuda/server.py`) uses `score_labels_many` when the engine has it and there are several questions; otherwise it keeps the per-question loop.
- **`MultiDecoder._pass_rows`** (`families/qwen4_exp/cuda/multi.py`): while a decision fills, a round's prompt pass is not share-limited. A decision waits on its whole prompt and nothing after it; share-sized pieces between rounds made three short prompts take ~0.9 s beside decoding chats.

## Measured (one DGX Spark, GB10; MLX 4-bit checkpoint, `--parallel 5`, int8 KV, v0.6.1 + this branch)

A decision request of 2 or 3 choice questions (4 to 7 options, ~150 tokens of prompt each):

| | 1 question | 2 questions | 3 questions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle server, median | 265 ms | 368 ms (2-question schema: 428 ms with 7 + 5 options) | 457–470 ms |
| Beside 1 / 2 decoding chats (3 questions) | | | 542–577 / 608 ms |

The 3 prompts fill in one pass (`rows=458 pieces=3`, 0.415 s). A prompt pass has a large fixed cost at this size
(1,100 tok/s at 458 rows against 1,730 at 4,096), which is most of the request. With `--parallel 5` and 3 decoding chats, a third question waits for a free slot (two passes, ~0.9 s).

## Checks

- **Same bits alone and grouped:** each question's probabilities alone equal the same question's in a 3-question request (9/9 cases), and a request beside 2 decoding chats equals the same request on an idle server.
- **Chats unchanged:** greedy outputs of our fixed 5-prompt fingerprint are byte-identical with and without this branch.
- **CPU tests:** `tests/test_flash_next_decisions.py` (collector; the route scores every question in one call, and falls
  back to one by one without `score_labels_many`) plus `tests/test_decisions.py` and `tests/test_cuda_server_errors.py`: 241 passed, 2 skipped.
- **Not tested:** two ranks (`--tp 2`, refused as for logprobs), image inputs in a decision, a CUDA test under `tests/cuda`.

## Context

We use it to route an assistant's messages before the answer (does it need the user's records, how to fetch them,
which period): on 43 labelled messages, the decisions matched the labels 43/43, 24/25 and 24/25, against three constrained generations before at 400–720 ms.

items.title: feat(cuda): add Flash Next image input and offline EXL3 vision adapter
items.body:
Enable image prompts for the Flash Next CUDA engine on one GPU with `--parallel 2` or more. Stock v0.5.0 restricts its vision path to dense Qwen3.5, while Flash Next needs feature injection across hyperconnection streams and multimodal positions in sparse attention.

This is an image-only port of MiaAI-Lab patch 0008, adapted to v0.5 forward/scheduler/grammar APIs with attribution and the original MIT license. It adds image-row embeddings, interleaved mRoPE and decode offsets, pooled-key positions, frontend/family validation and tower admission/warmup. Image states never enter the text-prefix cache; equal placeholder IDs are insufficient to identify pixels. Video, distributed vision and yieldable image requests are excluded.

EXL3 vision sidecars need a separate offline adapter: reconstruct represented quantized weights into a hashed FP16 artifact, combine split QKV in preference to retained fused copies, trim configured MLP padding and load it explicitly via `TENSORFOLD_VISION_WEIGHTS`. Hash both source weights and config before following HF blob symlinks. Conversion is not part of cold serving startup. An external tower is counted once in admission. BF16 tower arithmetic differs from native EXL3 execution; this is not a claim of numerical identity.

Validation on DGX Spark/GB10:
- 157 relevant CPU tests passed; one optional test skipped.
- Independent vision CUDA suite: 16 passed, including chunk invariance, BF16/int8 KV, drafted-versus-serial output and image cache isolation.
- Combined with #124 and the consolidated EXL3 fix: 70 CUDA tests passed.
- Actual 4.05-bpw EXL3 pack with four 262K streams: loaded with the converted 0.84-GiB tower and passed color changes, counting, OCR, chart reading, two images and image follow-up (7/7).

This branch is based on v0.5.0 and is independent of #124 and #145. The native 4.05 pack additionally requires #145 for its consolidated n-gram layout. #124 overlaps the prefill functions and needs integration preserving its text snapshots while keeping image states uncached. Paired native control also passed 7/7 image fixtures. Full encoders on five identical processed-patch inputs had cosine similarity 0.997970–0.999716 and relative L2 difference 2.389–6.398%; this is close, not numerical identity or general vision quality parity. The reconstructed tower uses BF16 arithmetic versus native FP16 EXL3 execution.

Text regression with the combined branch: 20/20 coding, 10/10 tools, 10/10 JSON, 4/4 retrieval through 240K and 3/3 actual drafted/serial token sequences. Same-checkpoint arithmetic was 49/50 versus native EXL3 50/50 with matched 4096-token budgets; the runtime discrepancy remains under investigation and this PR does not claim universal parity. These fixes remain experimental and have not replaced our production service.

items.title: fix(qwen4_exp cuda): resume identical resends and thinking turns
items.body:
Fixes #98.

Flash Next kept each prompt's state at its end, and a resume needs a strictly shorter prefix. So an identical
resend, or a next turn with thinking on (which renders the last prompt token differently), always prefilled in
full. This keeps the entry at `len(prompt) - 1`, as the 27B does, for one stream, `--parallel` and `--tp 2`.

One DGX Spark, `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, 11.7K-token prompt, time to first token:

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same prompt again | 5.2 s | 0.07 s |
| Next turn, thinking on | 5.2 s | 0.13 s |
| Next turn, thinking off | 0.20 s | 0.20 s |

The same holds with `--parallel 4`, and every reply equals its `"draft": false` reply. The kept state is taken
inside the chunk that holds it, as the 27B's prefill does, so a prompt costs no extra forward.

items.title: glm5_next: 8-bit / group-32 checkpoints on Macs + lossless Q8_0 GGUF converter
items.body:
GLM-5.3-Flash's Mac loader already reads 2–8-bit MLX affine weights in groups of 32/64/128, but `check()` admits only 4-bit / 64. This PR admits every format the loader reads (CUDA unchanged). It also lets the loader read a checkpoint converted **without loss** from llama.cpp's Q8_0 GGUF, and adds that converter. Measurements on the result: #116.

**Why it's exact:** a Q8_0 block (32 int8 values q, one fp16 scale d) is exactly MLX's affine 8-bit format in groups of 32, with q + 128, scale d and bias −128·d (both fp16).

**What changes**
- `check()`:
  - On Macs, admits any base format in `config.BITS × config.GROUPS`.
  - The refusal message now names what each engine reads.
- The loader:
  - fp16 scales are widened to float32 once at load (exact). Otherwise MLX promotes them on every call, a measured ~4.5× slower MoE.
  - The indexer projections and the KDA low-rank / beta projections load as stored: quantized, or unquantized as a Q8_0 GGUF keeps them (`Dense`).
  - The KDA decay rate may be stored as `A` (= −`ssm_a`, exact) instead of `A_log`.
  - Non-bf16-scale embeddings are dequantized in float32 (exact d·q) and enter the stream as bf16.
- **Every quantized projection returns its input's dtype.** Float32 scales would otherwise promote bf16 inputs to float32 outputs, which the sparse-decode Metal kernel refuses past 2,051 tokens. This touches `Q.__call__`, the MLA absorb/unabsorb maps, `gather_qmm` in the MoE and `_gather_one_row`. It is a no-op for bf16 scales.
- `KDA._small` uses the quad-row kernel only for quantized projections.
- `tools/glm5_q8_0_gguf_to_mlx.py`:
  - reads the GGUF directly (numpy, memory-mapped);
  - maps `attn_k_b` / `attn_v_b` to `embed_q` / `unembed_out` (same quantization axis);
  - keeps F16 / F32 tensors as bf16 when exact, else float32;
  - `--verify` checks every tensor against the GGUF.
- A recipe section in `docs/recipes/glm-5.3-flash.md`.

**Checks**
- New `tests/test_glm5_q8_0.py` (8 tests):
  - The encoding is exact, including subnormal scales and q = ±127 / −128.
  - Dense tensors keep every value.
  - A tiny checkpoint re-encoded as the converter writes it is admitted on Macs and refused on CUDA.
  - It loads with the `Dense` / widened-scale / `A` paths.
  - Prefill agrees with decode.
  - `multi_row_exact`, and MTP drafts change speed only, on CPU and on Metal.
- Full suite on an M4 Mac (non-CUDA): **2,388 passed, 598 skipped**; `main` (9cd52ab) gives 2,380 / 598.
- **bf16 unchanged:** `glm5_fakes` logits are byte-identical to `main` on CPU and on GPU.
- **Real weights** (M3 Ultra, 512 GB):
  - A 310 GiB Q8_0 GGUF became 328.5 GiB in 85 shards in about 6 minutes.
  - `--verify` found all 1,383 tensors equal to the GGUF.
  - 365 GiB of weights resident.
  - Served prefill 270 / 365 / 361 / 338 tok/s at 512 / 4k / 8k / 32k; decode ≈ 20 tok/s flat to 32k.
  - Held-out quality in #116 (bf16 row).

**Notes**
- The GGUF has no MTP layer, so the converted model decodes without drafts. The recipe says so.
- Overlaps with #118 in `model.embed_tokens`, `KDA._small` and `load_layer`; merging both is mechanical. `embed_tokens` should cast to `C.act()`.

*Prepared with the help of an AI assistant (Claude); I have reviewed the change and the measurements.*

**AI disclosure:** the code in this PR was written by Opus 5.5.

items.title: fix: stream tool-call arguments from the CUDA server
items.body:
The CUDA server sends nothing while a tool call is being written. A reply that writes a whole file in one `write` call streams no bytes until the reply ends, so clients with an idle timeout drop it: pi through LiteLLM, and Node's `fetch` (undici), both cut the body after ~300 s of silence and report `terminated`. The harness retries, the same prompt regenerates the same call, and it fails again at the same place.

This is the second half of #99, which its author closed. That PR sent empty keepalive deltas. This one streams the call's arguments as they are written, the way the Mac server already does, so the client sees progress and gets the call without waiting for the end parser. References are at `main` (7a00336).

## Cause

`App.run` hides tool-call markup from the answer (`src/tensorfold/cuda/server.py:304`), `on_tokens` emits only visible text (`:332`), and the handler sends the calls only after `run` returns (`:532`). The Mac server feeds the answer into `ToolCallStreamer` and emits its deltas as they arrive (`src/tensorfold/server/app.py:431`). The CUDA server never got that step.

## The change

- `run` builds a `ToolCallStreamer(tools)` when the request has tools and allows parallel calls. Each round it feeds the raw answer (never the reasoning) and emits the streamer's deltas after the visible-text delta: a header with the call's `id` and `name`, then `arguments` pieces.
- `run` returns `calls_streamed`, the number of calls already sent. The handler sends only the calls after those, i.e. the ones the streamer could not follow, from the end parser as before.
- Requests with `parallel_tool_calls: false` keep the end parser, which picks their single call (#21).
- The cancellation check still runs every round, with or without new text.

## Tests

- `tests/test_cuda_tool_choice.py`: the streamed required call now arrives as one header naming `get_weather` followed by argument deltas that join to `{"city": "Oslo"}`. A new test checks that `parallel_tool_calls: false` still sends the call in one piece.
- `tests/test_cuda_stop_strings.py`: the streaming helper merges argument deltas by index. The stop-string test that puts a second call after `STOP` still gets only the first call, so a call past the cut does not stream.

On macOS the full suite gives 2956 passed, 701 skipped. On a DGX Spark (NVIDIA PyTorch 26.07), the 21 files that exercise the CUDA server and `ToolCallStreamer` give 649 passed, 15 skipped, against 648 on `main`; the extra one is the new test.

## On the GPU

One DGX Spark (GB10), `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, `--parallel 3 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8 --mtp-drafts 6 --mtp-confidence 0.60 --ple-on-ssd`. One streamed request offering a `write(path, content)` tool, asking for a single-file Breakout game in one call:

| Thinking off | `main` (7a00336) | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| reply | 16,170 tokens, 220 s | 16,170 tokens, 223 s |
| first tool-call bytes | 220.1 s | 0.9 s |
| longest gap between SSE events | 219.4 s | 0.7 s |
| tool-call chunks | 1 | 4,123 |
| the call | `index.html`, 47,443 chars | the same bytes |

The two replies are identical: the change sends the same tokens, only earlier. With thinking on, this branch streamed 25k characters of reasoning, then the call from 156 s to the end at 517 s (35,035 tokens, a 71,617-character file) with no gap over 0.5 s. On `main` that call's 361 s would pass silent, over the ~300 s idle cut of Node's `fetch` and LiteLLM.

## Not covered

- A non-streamed reply still sends its headers only when done.
- A very long prefill before the first token is still silent.
- `parallel_tool_calls: false` requests still hold their call until the reply ends.

items.title: Fix #98: engage CUDA prefix retention on Flash Next (keep cache entry one token early)
items.body:
Fixes #98.

## Problem

On the CUDA lane, Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) remembered the **whole prompt** as its prefix-cache entry and matched only an exact token-prefix-extension. Flash Next is a reasoning model, so the next turn re-renders the assistant boundary (a stripped `<think>` plus two newlines), which changes the **last token** of the previous prompt. The stored full-prompt entry is then no longer a prefix of the next turn, `_slot_for` / `_resume` find nothing, `cached = 0`, and every turn pays a full prefill — exactly what #98 reports.

It reproduces only with **thinking on** (the default): with the reasoning boundary the last token diverges by exactly one token (`…assistant\n` → `…assistant\n<think>\n\n…`); with thinking off the full-prompt entry already matches.

## Fix

The dense 27B (`qwen3_5`) already avoids this by keeping its cache entry **one token early** (`entry_end`). This ports the same idea to `qwen4_exp`:

- `decode.prefill` gains `keep_at`: it forces a chunk boundary onto `keep_at`, captures the committed state there (a `resume` dict `{state, tail}`), then absorbs token `keep_at` into the MTP head exactly as a resume does. The kept state's bits match a fresh `prefill(prompt[:keep_at])` and the current request is unchanged; it returns `(first, kept)` when `keep_at` is set.
- `engine.entry_end` + both remember paths (concurrent `MultiDecoder.admit` and single-stream `_decode`) store `prompt[:entry_end]` with that early state. `entry_end` is applied on one GPU only, so the two-rank path (which hands rank 1 a fixed resume point) is untouched.

Output stays exact regardless: every drafted token is verified against the target and the reused KV rows come from the retained slot, so a wrong MTP resume tail could only lower draft acceptance, never change the reply.

## Results

1× DGX Spark (GB10), `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, `--parallel 5 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8`, thinking on. Controlled A/B: clean `v0.5.0` (worktree at `9cd52ab`) vs the same + this patch, identical image and flags.

| ctx | prompt toks | PP tok/s | TG tok/s | cold TTFT | warm TTFT (this PR) | speedup | cached toks | answer correct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2k   | 1,989   | 1,912 | 53.8 | 1.04 s   | 0.316 s | 3×   | 1,988   | yes |
| 16k  | 15,782  | 2,214 | 55.2 | 7.13 s   | 0.193 s | 37×  | 15,781  | yes |
| 64k  | 65,222  | 2,154 | 67.0 | 30.28 s  | 0.198 s | 153× | 65,221  | yes |
| 128k | 131,166 | 1,985 | 61.1 | 66.09 s  | 0.205 s | 323× | 131,165 | yes |
| 200k | 206,917 | 1,839 | 51.4 | 112.50 s | 0.216 s | 521× | 206,916 | yes |

- **Before (stock v0.5.0, same config):** `cached = 0` and warm TTFT = cold TTFT (1×) at every size — full re-prefill each turn.
- `cached` = prompt − 1 confirms the one-token-early entry.
- **Correctness:** a fact buried at ~80% depth is retrieved correctly on the resumed turn at every size up to 200k (thinking on and off); output is deterministic on re-run; draft acceptance on a resumed turn is not degraded (57% vs 53% cold).
- **No regression:** cold PP/TG match the unpatched build; `tools/bench.py` decode 69.3 code / 55.7 chat tok/s; `tools/toolcheck.py` OK.
- Validated on both CUDA paths: concurrent (`--parallel 4/5`) and single-stream (`--parallel 1`).

## Not in this change (follow-ups)

- Message-start snapshots via `resume_points` / `points` (needs multi-stop capture in `prefill`), for reuse when an earlier turn is edited.
- Resuming past the previous reply (this reuses up to the prompt end, one token early, like `qwen3_5`).
- The two-rank path.

items.title: perf: Flash Next lists QSA blocks past 131,072 keys in tiles (256k prompts 2.1x faster, same bits)
items.body:
**TL;DR: prompts past 131,072 tokens no longer slow down sharply, with the same bits and no setting to change.** A 250k-token prompt on one DGX Spark takes 143-145 s instead of 306-311 s. Up to 131,072 keys nothing changes.

## The problem

Flash Next's QSA selection (`_select` in `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/attention.py`) holds a row's block scores in registers: `next_pow2(blocks)` values a row, one 4-key block each. Up to 32,768 blocks (131,072 keys) that fits. Past it the array spills to local memory, and the kernel gets about 34x slower from one position to the next. One layer, one 256-row prompt block, one DGX Spark:

| Keys | `_scores` | `_select` | attention |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 65,536 | 0.84 ms | 0.20 ms | 1.31 ms |
| 131,072 | 1.66 ms | 0.78 ms | 2.24 ms |
| 135,168 | 1.72 ms | **26.41 ms** | 2.36 ms |
| 262,144 | 3.31 ms | **27.21 ms** | 2.93 ms |

A 256k-token prompt runs its second half as 512 row blocks x 12 QSA layers at ~27 ms each: about 165 s, half of its prefill. Decode windows past 131,072 keys pay it too (0.51 ms a layer at 7 rows).

## The change

`_select_tiles` lists the same blocks for rows with more blocks than `_select`'s registers hold. It reads the row in tiles (4,096 blocks for a prompt's row blocks, 8,192 for decode windows). It finds the same cut, the 512th largest order-preserving key, by radix select: one byte a pass from the top, with `tl.histogram` over the keys that share the cut's leading bytes. Then it places every key above the cut, and the lowest-id keys equal to it, in block order, exactly as `_select` does. `_launch_select` keeps `_select` while a row fits its registers, so every row up to 131,072 keys runs the same kernel as before.

| Keys | `_select` | `_select_tiles` |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 135,168, 256-row prompt block | 26.41 ms | 0.69 ms |
| 262,144, 256-row prompt block | 27.21 ms | 1.51 ms |
| 262,144, 7-row decode window | 0.51 ms | 0.25 ms |

## Results

One DGX Spark, MLX 4-bit checkpoint.

In one process with a 262,144-token cache (`select_ab`: the release's selection and this PR's, same engine):

| Prompt | 0.3.6.3 | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 250k tokens of prose, bf16 KV | 311.4 s | **145.0 s** |
| 250k tokens of prose, int8 KV (this PR first) | 306.4 s | **143.4 s** |
| 140k tokens of code, int8 KV (this PR first) | 86.3 s | **73.8 s** |

Served: `--parallel 2 --context 262144 --kv-dtype int8`, prompt to first token (sparkDash's prefill ladder). The "before" column is 0.3.6.2, whose `attention.py` is 0.3.6.3's.

| Prompt | Before | This PR |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8k | 3.4 s | 3.3 s |
| 32k | 13.1 s | 13.1 s |
| 256k | 300.9 s | **130.3 s** |

`llm_context_benchmarks` (ivanfioravanti), same server, real prose and Python at 256k:

| Prompt | Before | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| prose, prompt tok/s | 783 | **1,714** |
| code, prompt tok/s | 805 | **1,713** |

## Checks

- New test `test_qsa_rows_past_the_register_width_list_the_same_blocks`: a 7-row decode window and a 256-row prompt block, rows straddling 131,072 keys, 200k keys and the full 262,151-slot cache. It covers real, tied and all-equal scores, and checks two things: `_launch_select`'s lists equal `_select`'s at full width, and they equal the plain reference (the 512 best blocks, lower ids among equal scores, in block order, then the tail).
- In one process, bf16 and int8 KV: the state after 140k- and 250k-token prompts is identical with both selections. That covers the first token, the last row's streams, the DeltaNet states and conv windows, the n-gram tail, every KV, indexer and pooled cache, and the MTP caches (82 tensors). So are 64 drafted tokens after the 140k prompt, greedy and sampled.
- Flash Next CUDA and CPU tests: 364 passed, 11 skipped (Metal-only modules, optional EXL3 and kernel modules), 0 failed.
- Teacher-forced NLL through the prompt and the decode path: 119,980 of 119,980 values equal to the values stored from release 0.3.5.1.
- Server, bf16 KV, two streams at 262,144: 55 replayed benchmark replies (GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval) byte-identical to the replies stored from an earlier release. Repeat, concurrent and drafted-vs-serial each 9/9. Needles at 6k, 16k, 60k, 140k and 250k found 15/15.
- Server, int8 KV: repeat and concurrent 9/9.

items.title: fix: the CUDA server types Qwen tool parameters by the tool's schema
items.body:
**TL;DR:** on CUDA, a Qwen tool call's array, object, number and boolean parameters reach the client as JSON *strings*. With this change they arrive as typed JSON values, as the Mac server has returned them since 0.3.5 (#28). It changes 6 lines in `cuda/reply_text.py` and reuses the Mac server's `decode_parameter`.

## The problem

Qwen3.8 writes tool calls as `<function=name><parameter=k>value</parameter></function>`. The Mac server decodes each value by the tool's JSON schema (`tool_parameters.decode_parameter`, from #28). `cuda/reply_text.parse_tool_calls` never got that step and keeps every value as text. For example, a research agent's `finish(paths: array)` call on a DGX Spark (0.3.6.2, Qwen3.8 Flash Next, MLX 4-bit):

```
before: {"paths":"[\"https://a.example/1\", \"https://b.example/2\"]"}
after:  {"paths":["https://a.example/1","https://b.example/2"]}
```

Clients that validate arguments against the schema reject the call, and clients that don't pass a string where the tool expects a list.

## The change

`parse_tool_calls` builds `parameter_schemas(tools)` once per reply. Each `<parameter>` value then goes through `decode_parameter(value, schema)`, the same function and rules the Mac server uses:
- array, object, boolean, integer, number and null parameters decode when the text is valid JSON of that type;
- anything else keeps its exact text, including strings, untyped parameters, parameters missing from the schema, and text that isn't valid JSON of the declared type.

JSON-bodied and GLM calls are unchanged: they were already typed.

## Tests

- `tests/test_tool_parameter_types.py`: the existing parametrized check (8 kinds × 3 stream steps) now also runs the CUDA parser, with and without `max_calls`.
- `tests/test_glm_tool_calls.py::test_qwen_function_blocks_are_unchanged`: this test pinned the difference ("the CUDA server keeps them as text", added in 1fc5915). It now expects `days: 3` from both parsers. If that difference was deliberate, say so and I'll rework this.
- Without the fix, the updated tests fail 16 cases; with it they pass.
- Tool-call and server tests in `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.07-py3` (`test_tool_*`, `test_glm_tool_calls`, `test_cuda_tool_choice`, `test_cuda_server_stream`, `test_server_openai_compat`): **132 passed, 5 skipped, 2 failed**. The 2 failures are in `test_tool_parameters_null.py::test_http_*` and fail the same way on unmodified `main`, because they import `mlx`, which isn't available on Linux.
- Live check on one DGX Spark (`tensorfold serve Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP --parallel 4 --kv-dtype int8`): a `finish(paths: array)` call returns `paths` as a JSON array, both streamed and non-streamed.

items.title: feat: a quantized KV cache for Flash Next on CUDA (--kv-dtype int8 or int4)
items.body:
TensorFold's Flash Next CUDA engine can now keep its KV cache in 8 or 4 bits instead of bf16, behind a flag. The command is `tensorfold serve MODEL --kv-dtype int8` (or `int4`). The default stays bf16, so nothing changes for an existing command, and the MLX path refuses anything but bf16 because this only exists on CUDA.

What you get is memory, not speed. On one DGX Spark the 8-bit cache is 1.68x smaller than bf16 and decodes at the same speed on short prompts, a few percent faster once the prompt is a few thousand tokens. The 4-bit cache is 3.17x smaller, costs about 12% decode speed at short context, and is roughly even by 4,000 tokens. Both change the output. I measured how much, and the numbers are below rather than summarized.

This is the same scheme ExLlamaV3 uses for `-cq 8` and `-cq 4` (the default grid, no companding): groups of 32 along the head dim, the group rotated by a 32-point Hadamard, one fp16 scale per group taken as the group's absmax, and a midpoint grid. 4-bit packs two codes per byte. The indexer keys and the pooled block keys stay bf16, so the saving applies to the K and V tensors only. The query is rotated on the way in and the merged attention output on the way out, which lets the stored keys and values stay in the rotated domain instead of being rotated back on every read.

## What changed

- `cd90ecc`, the 8-bit cache. `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/kvcache.py` is new and holds the storage, the Hadamard, and the quantize and dequantize kernels, plus a pure-torch reference quantizer that the tests check against. `glue.py` quantizes keys and values as it writes the cache and rotates the query. `attention.py` dequantizes inside the attention kernel and rotates the merged output back. `forward.py`, `decode.py` and `engine.py` thread the dtype through, and the MTP drafter's own cache uses the same dtype as the main cache, so drafts and verification see the same representation. `cli.py` gains `--kv-dtype {bf16,int8,int4}`, CUDA only.
- `710ad04`, the 4-bit cache, on the same path. One `bits` parameter runs through the kernels rather than a second copy of them. The quantize and dequantize each had to be split into per-width kernels: Triton compiles every branch of a function, and a shared function returned a different shape at 4 bits (two codes per byte) than at 8, which broke compilation of the 8-bit path. `attention.py` loads the packed nibbles and unpacks before the dot.
- `09eb756`, `--mtp-confidence` on the CUDA serve path. The draft chain stops early once a draft's probability drops below this, and the default is 0.3. I added it because the speed numbers people quote for this model were measured at 0.6, and there was no way to ask for that. It is included here because the measurements below depend on it.
- `33a151e` and `05b49a8`, the tests. `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kvquant.py` checks both widths: the kernels write the reference quantizer's bits exactly, the scales match ExLlamaV3's own quantizer, the cache round-trips inside the grid, attention output stays within a stated tolerance of bf16, a window of rows matches the same rows computed one at a time, chunked prefill matches one shot, drafted decoding matches serial by token-id SHA-256, and the end-to-end logits stay close to bf16. `tests/test_cuda_cli.py` covers the flag parsing, including the refusal on the MLX path.
- `139b0a4` and `1f4131e`, the docs. `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md` gains a section on the flag, the README's option list names it, and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` credits the scheme to ExLlamaV3 (MIT, Copyright (c) 2025 Turboderp).

13 files, +920 / -49, 8 commits, no merge commits, based on `bb4b4a3`.

## Measured on a GB10 (DGX Spark)

One DGX Spark (GB10, driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.11, 128 GB unified). Every timing arm ran in an exclusive session with the GPU otherwise idle. The model is `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, the MLX 4-bit affine checkpoint (group size 32) with MTP drafting. It is not an EXL3 checkpoint. This branch is cut from upstream `main`, and upstream cannot load EXL3 packs. That is what #42 adds, so the EXL3 numbers and these are not comparable and I have not mixed them.

### Memory

Bytes per token for one attention layer's K and V plus the fp16 scales, head dim 256, 2 KV heads. The scales are included. Leaving them out overstates the saving, and the whole-cache figure is the one that matters:

| cache | bytes/token/layer | vs bf16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 2,048 | 1.00x |
| int8 | 1,088 | 1.88x |
| int4 | 576 | 3.56x |

Across the whole model the saving is smaller, because the indexer keys and the pooled block keys stay bf16 either way. For Flash Next that works out to 1.68x at int8 (30,784 bytes per token down to 18,304) and 3.17x at int4. At a 262,144-token context the K and V pool drops from 7.52 GiB to 4.47 GiB at int8.

### Speed

Drafted decode, greedy, 400 tokens, median of 3 reps, thinking off. Depth 6 with confidence 0.6 is the policy, and depth 7 at 0.75 is the single best point I measured. SM clock was 2502 to 2528 MHz of a 3003 max during decode, so these are not peak-clock numbers. The client is the same for every arm.

Short prompts, 8,192-token context, tok/s:

| cache | code | devops | prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 86.76 | 64.45 | 52.27 |
| int8 | 85.17 | 64.25 | 53.84 |
| int4 | 76.73 | 59.79 | 50.61 |

Depth 7 at confidence 0.75, code prompt only: bf16 88.16, int8 87.16, int4 77.88.

A 4,121-token prompt in a 32,768-token context, depth 6 at confidence 0.6. Here the reps are tight enough to trust the gap, so I list them:

| cache | median | the three reps | prefill, tok/s |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| bf16 | 75.44 | 74.18, 75.44, 75.60 | 158.3 |
| int8 | 79.72 | 78.14, 79.72, 79.78 | 158.0 |
| int4 | 76.14 | 74.74, 76.14, 76.22 | 158.4 |

Read together: at short context the dequantize costs more than the bandwidth saves, so int8 is a wash (about 98% of bf16) and int4 gives up about 12% on code. By 4,000 tokens of context int8 is 5.7% faster and its slowest rep beat bf16's fastest, while int4 is even with bf16, inside the noise. Prefill is identical across all three, which is what you would expect, since prefill is dominated by the weights and not the cache.

### Quality

Teacher-forced, 2,048 positions from the pack's own bench corpus, full vocabulary, the KL summed in fp32. The same weights in every arm, only the cache dtype changes. NLL is in bits per token.

| cache | NLL | top-1 | KL vs bf16, mean | KL p50 | KL p95 | KL max | top-1 agreement vs bf16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 2.7613 | 0.6680 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| int8 | 2.8217 | 0.6665 | 0.2093 | 0.0119 | 1.133 | 11.31 | 0.8916 |
| int4 | 2.7198 | 0.6636 | 0.3911 | 0.0244 | 2.146 | 17.44 | 0.8662 |

The floor of this measurement is zero in the only sense I could test. I scored the bf16 cache, reloaded the model, and scored it again: same NLL to the digit, KL of 0. The engine is deterministic, so the KL above is the cache and not run-to-run noise. I had first tried to get a floor by varying the prefill chunk size, and that came back as zero too, but for a bad reason: the chunk size never reaches the forward pass, so the two arms were the same run. I am not using that zero.

Two things about this table that are easy to misread. The median KL is small (0.012 bits at int8, 0.024 at int4) while the mean is large, which means most positions barely move and a few move a lot. And int4's NLL is lower than bf16's. That is not int4 being more accurate. A quantized cache shifts the distribution, and a lower NLL on one corpus is a sign of that shift, not a quality win. Top-1 agreement is the cleaner summary: int8 keeps the bf16 top token on 89.2% of positions, int4 on 86.6%.

## Tests

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kvquant.py   # 30 collected
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py   # 16 passed
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kernels.py   # 35 passed
```

`test_flashnext_kvquant.py` holds 30 tests across the two widths. The checks that matter:

- the kernels write exactly the bits the reference quantizer does, at 8 and at 4 bits, and the scales match ExLlamaV3's own quantizer on the same groups;
- the cache round-trips inside the grid, and packing then unpacking 4-bit codes returns the same codes;
- attention over a quantized cache stays within a stated tolerance of attention over bf16;
- a window of rows matches the same rows computed one at a time (`torch.equal`), and chunked prefill matches one shot;
- drafted decoding matches serial decoding by token-id SHA-256, through `tensorfold serve`, at both widths;
- the end-to-end logits stay close to the bf16 cache.

The host suite, run with the same exclusions as upstream (`--ignore=tests/test_alternating_kv.py --ignore=tests/test_dflash_tree_search.py`), shows the same 4 failures and 130 passes as `upstream/main`. Those 4 are environmental (this box has no MLX) and are present on main.

## Overlap with open PRs

`git merge-tree` is clean against `upstream/main`. It is also clean against #42 (`pr/exl3`), even though the two branches both edit `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md`, `README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/forward.py`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/__init__.py` and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. The edits are in different regions and merge without help. I will rebase on #42 if it lands first.

#40 also touches `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/{attention,decode,engine,forward}.py`, and #29 touches `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md` and the MLX-side decode path. I have not merge-tested those two. Both are small overlaps and I will rebase on whichever lands first.

This also answers the request in #23, partly. That issue is a GLM model running out of memory at 64k on two Sparks and asks for an fp8 cache or a `--kv-dtype`. The flag is the one asked for, but the implementation covers Flash Next only. GLM, the 27B and MiMo are not included, and I do not have a GLM checkpoint here to test against.

## What is not claimed

- No long context past 4,121 tokens. I measured at short prompts and at one 4,121-token prompt. 24k, 128k and 262k are not measured. The memory math above says they fit, and the speed there is an extrapolation from the 4k result, not a measurement.
- No EXL3 checkpoint. Everything here is the MLX 4-bit pack. The EXL3 packs need #42, and the speeds in #42 and the speeds here are different models measured on different branches.
- No peak-clock numbers. The SM clock sat at 2502 to 2528 MHz of a 3003 max during these runs. A pinned clock would read higher, and I have not measured by how much.
- int4 is not faster. It is smaller. At short context it is slower than bf16 by about 12% on code, and at 4,000 tokens it is even. Its reason to exist is the 3.17x memory cut, and it costs 13.4 points of top-1 agreement to get there.
- The quality numbers are one corpus of 2,048 positions, teacher-forced. They say how far the distribution moves, not how that shows up in generated text. I did not run a side-by-side generation comparison.
- The indexer keys and pooled block keys are not quantized, so a model whose cache is dominated by those would see a smaller saving than the table suggests. Flash Next is not such a model, but GLM might be, and I have not checked.
